It is positioned as a successor to VP9 and a competitor to HEVC, and it is widely cited as offering meaningful compression gains over older standards such as H.264 and VP8 at the same visual quality. Those gains are attractive for RTC, but they come at the cost of higher computational complexity, which is the central tension Meta describes navigating throughout the effort.

According to the company, the work began with codec selection, weighing AV1 against the codecs already deployed in its calling infrastructure. Streaming services have adopted AV1 primarily for video on demand, where encoding can be performed offline and decoders have time to buffer. Real-time communication is different: the encoder and decoder both run live, latency budgets are measured in milliseconds, and there is no opportunity to re-encode. This means the theoretical compression advantage of AV1 must be balanced against whether a device can sustain real-time encoding and decoding without overheating, draining battery, or dropping frames.

Device eligibility is therefore a recurring theme. Meta explains that not every phone or computer can run AV1 in real time, particularly on the encode path, which is more demanding than decode. The company appears to rely on a tiering or gating approach, enabling AV1 only where a device has sufficient hardware or software capability and falling back to other codecs otherwise. Hardware AV1 decode support has been expanding in newer mobile chipsets and GPUs, while software decoders such as dav1d are used to broaden compatibility where hardware support is absent. On the encoding side, real-time-oriented implementations are needed, since reference encoders like libaom were designed with quality and offline use in mind rather than the speed RTC requires.

Rate control is another pillar of the work. In real-time calls, the available bandwidth fluctuates constantly as users move between networks, and the encoder must adjust its bitrate moment to moment to avoid congestion and latency spikes. Meta notes that it had to adapt rate control specifically for AV1's characteristics so that the codec responds quickly to bandwidth estimates from the transport layer. This is closely tied to techniques common in modern RTC systems, including scalable video coding and simulcast, which let a sender produce multiple quality layers so that participants on different connections each receive an appropriate stream.

Error resilience rounds out the technical agenda. Real-time media is typically carried over unreliable transport, so packet loss is expected rather than exceptional. Unlike a streaming player that can pause and rebuffer, an RTC system must keep the picture moving through lost or late packets. Meta describes investing in resilience so that AV1 streams degrade gracefully under loss, using mechanisms to limit error propagation and recover quickly rather than freezing the video.

The broader context is an industry-wide shift toward AV1 in interactive media. The codec has been integrated into the WebRTC ecosystem, browsers have added support, and several large platforms have signaled interest in using it for conferencing as hardware acceleration becomes more common. Meta's account is notable mainly for the scale and the operational detail, covering not just compression results but the practical questions of how to deploy a demanding codec across a heterogeneous fleet of consumer devices.

Meta frames the project as ongoing rather than finished, and the published findings are likely intended both to document its engineering choices and to inform others working on similar systems. As more devices ship with native AV1 acceleration, the trade-offs the company outlines around eligibility and complexity should ease, potentially making efficient, royalty-free real-time video more widely available across the industry.

e5df8f409651f25f.bodyJa:
Google Cloud は、BigQuery でマネージド Python UDF（ユーザー定義関数）を一般提供（GA）したと発表した。これにより、これまで SQL だけでは表現が難しかった複雑な手続き型ロジックや科学計算、機械学習（ML）処理を、慣れ親しんだ SQL クエリと組み合わせて直接実行できるようになる。

SQL は構造化データの高速分析において事実上の業界標準だが、繰り返しや条件分岐を伴う複雑な処理、高度な文字列操作、統計・科学計算、ML 推論といった用途では表現力に限界がある。従来も BigQuery は SQL UDF や JavaScript UDF を提供してきたが、データ分析やサイエンスの分野で広く使われる Python を、ライブラリ群とともにそのまま活用したいという需要は大きかった。

マネージド Python UDF は、その名の通りランタイムや実行基盤を Google Cloud 側が管理する点が特徴とされる。利用者はインフラの構築や運用を意識せずに Python のコードを関数として定義し、SQL から呼び出せる。PyPI などの外部パッケージを取り込み、NumPy や pandas のような科学計算ライブラリを処理に組み込める設計と見られ、ETL の前処理から特徴量エンジニアリング、推論まで幅広いワークロードに応用できる可能性がある。

この動きは、データウェアハウスに分析言語としての Python を統合する近年の潮流の延長線上にある。Snowflake は Snowpark を通じて Python による処理を、Databricks も Spark 基盤上で Python を提供しており、各社が SQL と Python の両立を競っている。Google Cloud 自身も、pandas 互換の操作を BigQuery 上で実行する BigQuery DataFrames（BigFrames）や、SQL から ML モデルを扱う BigQuery ML を展開してきた。今回の GA は、こうしたエコシステムにおいて Python を「補助的な拡張」から「第一級の処理手段」へと位置づけ直す一歩といえる。

GA への移行により、本番環境での利用を前提とした安定性やサポートが期待できる。一方で、実際の性能やコスト、対応するパッケージの範囲、同時実行時の制約などは利用ケースによって異なるため、導入にあたっては自社のワークロードでの検証が重要になりそうだ。
e5df8f409651f25f.bodyEn:
Google Cloud has announced the general availability of managed Python user-defined functions (UDFs) in BigQuery, letting data teams run Python code directly inside SQL queries without provisioning or maintaining separate infrastructure. The change matters because it narrows a long-standing gap between SQL, the dominant language for structured analytics, and Python, the de facto language for data science, machine learning, and scientific computing.

SQL is widely regarded as the industry standard for high-performance analysis over structured data, but it is not well suited to expressing complex procedural logic, advanced string manipulation, numerical routines, or model inference. Teams have historically handled these tasks by exporting data to external environments, building separate pipelines, or wiring together additional services. Managed Python UDFs are designed to reduce that friction by letting a developer define a function in Python and call it from a standard SQL statement, with BigQuery handling the execution.

The functions run in a managed, serverless runtime that BigQuery provisions automatically, so users do not need to configure containers, clusters, or virtual machines. A developer writes a Python function, declares any required dependencies, and BigQuery packages and runs the code at query time, scaling resources as needed. Because the environment supports installing packages from the Python Package Index, common libraries such as NumPy, pandas, and scikit-learn can be used within a function. That makes it possible to perform scientific calculations, custom transformations, or lightweight machine-learning inference in the same query that filters and aggregates the underlying tables.

This is not BigQuery's first mechanism for extending SQL. The service already supported user-defined functions written in SQL and JavaScript, as well as remote functions that invoke external endpoints on Cloud Run or Cloud Functions. The distinction with managed Python UDFs is that the Python execution is handled inside the BigQuery service rather than requiring developers to deploy and operate their own endpoint. That approach is intended to lower operational overhead, keep code governed within the data platform, and bring the computation closer to where the data resides.

The feature fits into a broader set of Python-oriented capabilities Google has been building around BigQuery. BigQuery DataFrames, often referred to as bigframes, offers a pandas- and scikit-learn-compatible Python API that pushes computation down into BigQuery's engine. BigQuery ML allows models to be trained and called using SQL, and the platform integrates with Vertex AI for more advanced model serving. Managed Python UDFs complement these tools by giving developers a way to embed arbitrary Python logic at the row or column level inside a query.

The announcement also reflects competitive dynamics in the cloud data warehouse market. Rivals have invested heavily in bringing Python closer to the warehouse, most visibly Snowflake with its Snowpark framework and Databricks with its Spark- and Python-centric lakehouse approach. Bringing a managed Python runtime into BigQuery appears to be part of Google's effort to keep data science and analytics workloads on a single platform rather than splitting them across separate

a2d5a7b277e97678.bodyJa:
Google は、AI 開発環境「Google AI Studio」で作成したプロトタイプを、ライブ URL として手軽に公開・共有できる「スターター ティア」を提供している。動くプロトタイプから実際に使えるアプリへと進む最初の一歩を埋める機能で、開発初期のスピードを重視する個人や小規模チームにとって有用と見られる。

Google AI Studio は、Gemini モデルを使ったアプリケーションのプロトタイピングを支援する開発環境だ。チャット形式でプロンプトを試したり、React によるフロントエンドや Node.js のバックエンド、さらにデータベースを組み合わせたアプリを組み立てたりできる。これまでは手元で動かしたプロトタイプを誰かに見せたい場合、別途ホスティング環境を用意してデプロイする手間が必要だった。

スターター ティアは、この「手元で動くもの」を「URL で共有できるもの」へと変える橋渡しの役割を担う。チームメンバーやユーザー、あるいは試してみたい友人に対して、リンクを送るだけで実際の動作を体験してもらえる。サーバーの構成やビルドの設定といったインフラ作業を最小限に抑え、アイデアの検証に集中できる点が特徴だ。

背景には、生成 AI を活用したアプリ開発の裾野が急速に広がっている状況がある。Vercel の v0 や Anthropic の Claude Artifacts、Replit など、コードの生成からデプロイまでを一気通貫で行えるサービスが相次いで登場しており、各社が「アイデアを即座に形にする」体験の磨き込みを競っている。Google にとってもスターター ティアは、AI Studio で生まれたアイデアを自社クラウド上の本格的な運用へとつなげる入り口になる可能性がある。

利用にあたっては、まず AI Studio 上でプロトタイプを構築し、公開操作を行うことでライブ URL が発行される流れが想定される。本格的な負荷や可用性が求められる段階では、Google Cloud の各種サービスへ移行する選択肢も考えられる。まずは素早く公開して反応を得たい開発者にとって、検証サイクルを短縮する実用的な選択肢といえそうだ。
a2d5a7b277e97678.bodyEn:
You have a working prototype in Google AI Studio: a React frontend, a Node.js backend, perhaps a small database wired into a Gemini model. The natural next step is to share it, and that usually means moving from a local development environment to something reachable on the open web. Google's Starter Tier for AI Studio is aimed squarely at that moment, offering a path to publish a prototype to a live, shareable URL without forcing developers to stand up their own hosting infrastructure first.

The core idea is to collapse the gap between building and deploying. AI Studio has grown beyond a place to test prompts; it now functions as a lightweight application builder, where developers can scaffold full-stack apps that call Gemini APIs and iterate on them in the browser. Historically, taking one of those apps from the editor to a deployment required exporting the code and configuring a separate service. The Starter Tier appears designed to shorten that loop, letting you turn a prototype into a hosted application that teammates, early users, or a curious friend can open in a browser.

According to the framing from Google, the typical project this targets is a conventional web stack: a React single-page frontend paired with a Node.js server that handles API calls, secrets, and any data persistence. Keeping server-side logic in Node.js matters here, because it allows API keys for Gemini and other services to stay on the backend rather than being exposed in client-side code. That separation is a basic security practice, and a managed deployment tier that preserves it is more useful for real testing than a frontend-only preview would be.

A live URL also changes how a prototype can be evaluated. Sharing a link instead of asking colleagues to clone a repository and run it locally lowers the barrier to feedback, which is often the slowest part of early product work. For demos, user interviews, or internal reviews, a hosted version that behaves like the eventual product gives more reliable signal than screenshots or a recorded walkthrough. The "starter" naming is likely deliberate, signaling that this is intended for prototypes and limited-audience testing rather than production traffic at scale, though the exact quotas, limits, and pricing are the kind of details developers should confirm against current documentation.

It helps to place this in the broader context of how Google has been positioning its AI developer tools. AI Studio sits alongside Vertex AI, the more enterprise-oriented platform where teams typically move when they need stronger governance, scaling, MLOps tooling, and integration with the rest of Google Cloud. AI Studio has generally served as the faster, lower-friction entry point, and a built-in deployment tier reinforces that role by letting people validate an idea before committing to heavier infrastructure. The underlying hosting is likely backed by Google Cloud's serverless offerings, such as Cloud Run, which already specialize in running containerized web services without server management, although the Starter Tier abstracts much of that away.

The move also reflects a wider industry pattern. Several AI platform providers have been adding one-click or low-configuration deployment so that AI-assisted coding does not stop at generated code. Tools and services in the same space, including app builders and AI coding assistants from other vendors, increasingly bundle hosting so that the output of a model-driven workflow can be experienced immediately. The competitive logic is straightforward: the faster a developer can see a working, shareable result, the more valuable the build experience feels, and the more likely a project is to advance.

For developers considering it, a few prerequisites are worth keeping in mind. Familiarity with React and Node.js remains the baseline, since the deployment assumes that stack. Anyone planning to graduate a prototype beyond initial sharing should think early about how data, authentication, and rate limits will scale, and whether the eventual home is Vertex AI or a custom Cloud deployment. As with any managed tier, it is sensible to review the current terms, regional availability, and any usage caps before relying on it for anything beyond experimentation. Treated as what its name suggests, a starting point, the tier appears to fill a practical gap between prototyping in AI Studio and operating a fully managed production service.

b99141870494857d.bodyJa:
Microsoftは、米テキサス州ペコス（Pecos）に新たなデータセンターを開設し、生成AIの普及で急増する計算需要に対応するためのインフラ容量を大幅に拡充したと発表した。同社のクラウド基盤を支える継続的な大型投資の一環であり、次世代AIサービスの土台を強化する動きとして位置づけられる。

近年、大規模言語モデルの学習や推論には膨大なGPUと電力が必要とされ、クラウド事業者は世界各地でデータセンターの新設・増床を急いでいる。MicrosoftはAzureを通じてOpenAIのモデルやCopilotなどのAI機能を提供しており、こうしたサービスの利用拡大が容量逼迫の背景にあると見られる。新拠点はそのボトルネックを緩和し、より多くのワークロードを受け入れる狙いがあるとみられる。

テキサス州は、比較的安価な土地や独自の電力網（ERCOT）、再生可能エネルギーの拡大などを背景に、近年データセンターの集積が進む地域の一つだ。一方で、AI向け施設は消費電力と冷却需要が大きく、地域の電力供給や水資源への影響が各地で議論の対象となっている。事業者は液冷技術の導入や再エネ調達、効率改善などで環境負荷の抑制を図る動きを見せている。

こうした投資競争はMicrosoftに限らない。Amazon（AWS）やGoogle、Metaなども相次いで巨額の設備投資を表明しており、AIインフラの確保が大手テック各社の中核戦略になっている。各社は半導体の調達やデータセンター用地の取得、長期の電力契約などで先行を競っている状況だ。

今回のPecos拠点が具体的にどの程度の規模や電力容量を持つのか、稼働時期などの詳細は限られている。ただ、Microsoftがこれまで示してきた一連の拡張計画と合わせて考えると、AI需要の長期的な拡大を見据えた供給能力の積み増しという流れの一部と捉えられる。今後も同社は地理的に分散した拠点網を広げ、AIワークロードの安定供給と冗長性の確保を進めていく可能性がある。
b99141870494857d.bodyEn:
Microsoft has announced a new datacenter in Pecos, Texas, positioning the facility as part of its drive to add capacity for the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence workloads. The move matters because the current wave of generative AI services, from large language models to enterprise assistants, depends on enormous amounts of computing power, and the companies that build and operate that infrastructure are effectively setting the pace at which AI products can scale.

According to the company's Source blog, the Pecos site is intended to expand the underlying capacity that powers AI services, and it is framed as one piece of a continuing program of investment rather than a standalone project. That framing is consistent with how Microsoft has described its broader strategy in recent years, in which datacenter construction is tied directly to demand for Azure cloud services and for AI features embedded across its product portfolio, including the Copilot assistants in Windows, Microsoft 365, and developer tools such as GitHub Copilot.

The choice of west Texas reflects several practical considerations that have made the region attractive to hyperscale operators. Pecos sits in the Permian Basin, an area with extensive open land, established energy infrastructure, and access to both conventional and renewable power. Texas operates its own electricity grid through ERCOT, which gives developers a degree of flexibility in negotiating power supply, though it also exposes facilities to the grid's well-documented stress during extreme weather. Large datacenters require substantial and reliable electricity, and the availability of generation capacity has become a central factor in deciding where to build.

The technical context behind such expansions is the shift toward AI-optimized infrastructure. Training and running modern AI models rely heavily on clusters of specialized accelerators, most commonly graphics processing units, interconnected by high-bandwidth networking. These systems consume significantly more power per rack than traditional server installations, which in turn drives demand for advanced cooling. Many newer facilities incorporate liquid cooling or other approaches designed to manage the heat generated by dense GPU deployments. While Microsoft has not detailed every specification of the Pecos site in the available summary, a facility built for the "next wave of AI" is likely to emphasize this kind of high-density, accelerator-focused design.

The announcement also fits within a broader industry pattern. Microsoft's principal cloud competitors, including Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, have committed to multibillion-dollar capital programs aimed at AI capacity, and Meta has likewise invested heavily in compute for its own models. Microsoft's relationship with OpenAI, which it has supported with dedicated infrastructure, has added further pressure to expand. Industry analysts have noted that capital expenditure among the largest cloud providers has climbed sharply, driven primarily by the need for AI hardware and the buildings to house it. Texas in particular has emerged as a focal point for this construction, with multiple operators citing its land and energy profile.

Resource use is an increasingly prominent part of the conversation around new datacenters. Power consumption and water use for cooling have drawn scrutiny from local communities, regulators, and environmental groups, especially in arid regions. Microsoft has publicly set sustainability goals, including commitments to become carbon negative and to reduce water consumption, and the company has experimented with cooling techniques intended to limit reliance on water. How a desert-region facility such as Pecos addresses cooling and water sourcing appears likely to be a point of interest as more details emerge, though the published summary does not specify the measures involved.

For customers and the wider market, additional capacity generally translates into greater availability for cloud and AI services, which can ease the supply constraints that have at times limited access to advanced computing resources. It is worth treating broad claims about transformative impact with caution, since the practical effect of any single site depends on factors such as timing, the hardware installed, and overall demand. Nonetheless, the Pecos datacenter underscores how heavily the future of AI services rests on physical infrastructure, and how decisions about land, power, and engineering are now inseparable from progress in software.

172a3c50f7e20874.bodyJa:
米国科学財団(NSF)が主導するNAIRR(National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource)パイロットプログラムが、運用開始からの約2年間で700件を超える研究プロジェクトを支援してきた。NVIDIAのAIインフラを基盤に据え、全米の研究者にAIコンピューティング資源へのアクセスを提供することで、科学研究の進め方を大きく変えつつある。

NAIRRは、AI研究に欠かせない計算資源やデータセット、ソフトウェアツールを広く共有するための国家的な構想だ。大規模なモデルの学習や推論には膨大なGPU計算が必要となるが、こうした設備は一部の大手テック企業や潤沢な予算を持つ研究室に偏りがちだった。NAIRRは、資金や設備の制約でAIを活用しにくかった研究者にも門戸を開き、研究機会の格差を縮める狙いがあるとされる。

技術面では、NVIDIAのGPUと関連するソフトウェアスタックが計算基盤の中核を担っているとみられる。同社はCUDAをはじめとする開発環境や、科学計算向けのライブラリ群を整備しており、創薬、気候変動、材料科学、天文学など幅広い分野で研究者がこれらを活用していると報告されている。近年は生成AIや基盤モデルを科学的発見に応用する動きも広がっており、シミュレーションとデータ駆動型のアプローチを組み合わせる研究が増えている。

こうした官民連携の枠組みは、国際的な競争のなかでも注目される。各国が国家規模のAI計算基盤、いわゆる「ソブリンAI」の整備を進めるなか、米国は特定の機関に偏らない研究エコシステム全体の底上げを図ろうとしている。一方で、NAIRRはあくまでパイロット段階であり、本格的な運用に向けた継続的な予算確保や制度設計は今後の課題となる可能性がある。

700件超という実績は、AIインフラへの公平なアクセスが科学研究の裾野を広げうることを示す一例といえる。今後、支援対象の拡大や成果の社会還元がどこまで進むかが、プログラムの真価を測る指標になりそうだ。
172a3c50f7e20874.bodyEn:
For the past two years, the U.S. National Science Foundation's National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, known as NAIRR, has functioned as a shared pilot program designed to broaden access to advanced computing for the scientific community. According to NVIDIA, the program has now supported more than 700 research projects across the United States, drawing on NVIDIA AI infrastructure to give academic and institutional researchers compute resources they might otherwise struggle to obtain. The effort matters because access to high-performance AI hardware has become a defining factor in who can pursue ambitious, data-intensive science.

NAIRR was conceived as a response to a widening gap. Frontier AI research increasingly depends on large clusters of accelerators, extensive datasets, and software tooling that are expensive to acquire and operate. Well-funded corporate labs and a handful of elite universities have had ready access to these resources, while many researchers at smaller institutions, minority-serving colleges, and underfunded departments have not. The NAIRR pilot, launched following recommendations from a federal task force, aims to distribute that capability more evenly by pooling contributions from government agencies and private-sector partners into a single, accessible platform.

The 700-plus supported projects reportedly span a wide range of disciplines. Such programs typically encompass work in areas like climate and weather modeling, materials discovery, drug and protein research, healthcare diagnostics, agriculture, and foundational machine learning methods. The common thread is that each project requires substantial computational throughput, whether for training models, running large-scale simulations, or analyzing complex datasets. By offering allocations of GPU time and associated tooling, the program lowers a practical barrier that has historically constrained where cutting-edge AI research can take place.

On the technical side, NVIDIA's contribution centers on its accelerated computing stack. This generally includes data-center GPUs alongside the CUDA software ecosystem, optimized libraries, and frameworks for training and deploying neural networks. NVIDIA has also promoted tools such as its inference microservices and domain-specific software for science, which can shorten the path from raw hardware to usable research workflows. The company's broader strategy has involved positioning its platforms as the underlying layer for what it describes as AI factories, large installations dedicated to producing model outputs at scale. NAIRR appears to extend that approach into the public research sphere.

It is worth situating the program within a larger national and industry context. The United States has treated AI capacity as a matter of economic competitiveness and scientific leadership, and NAIRR is one of several initiatives intended to keep domestic researchers at the frontier. It sits alongside the country's network of national laboratories and academic supercomputing centers, including facilities supported by the Department of Energy and NSF-funded systems accessed through programs like ACCESS. The pilot is structured to complement these resources rather than replace them, and it relies on commitments from multiple technology providers, not only NVIDIA, even though NVIDIA's hardware is dominant in current AI workloads.

The pilot also reflects a recurring pattern in which companies that supply AI hardware partner with public institutions to expand the ecosystem around their products. Such arrangements can accelerate research while also familiarizing a new generation of scientists with a particular vendor's tools, a dynamic that observers have noted across the sector. Whether the NAIRR pilot transitions into a permanent, fully funded national resource is likely to depend on legislative action and sustained budget support, which remain outside any single company's control.

For researchers, the practical significance lies in access. A scientist with a promising idea but no local GPU cluster can, in principle, apply for an allocation and proceed without building infrastructure from scratch. That model could help diversify who contributes to AI-enabled discovery and reduce duplication of costly hardware investments. At the same time, the long-term impact will hinge on factors such as allocation policies, ease of onboarding, data governance, and the program's eventual scale.

As the pilot phase matures, the figure of more than 700 projects offers an early indicator of demand. It suggests that shared, centrally provisioned AI infrastructure addresses a genuine need within the research community, and it positions NAIRR as a notable case study in how public agencies and private technology firms can collaborate to support science in an era increasingly shaped by computational capacity.

064f783eeb8d3cdf.bodyJa:
スマートフォン単体でローカルLLM（大規模言語モデル）を動かす——そんな実験的な取り組みを、プログラミング未経験者がAIアシスタントと二人三脚で進める連載記事の続編が、技術情報共有サービスZennで公開された。今回のテーマは、端末のカメラとモデルを連携させる仕組みと、開発でつまずきやすいデバッグの実際である。

連載では、GoogleがオンデバイスAI向けに提供する推論ランタイム「LiteRT-LM」を中核に据えている。LiteRTは、従来TensorFlow Liteと呼ばれていた軽量実行環境の後継にあたり、スマートフォンのような限られた計算資源でもモデルを動かせるよう最適化されている。前回の記事では、このエンジンのアーキテクチャや、テキスト・画像・音声といった複数の入力形式への対応が解説されていた。

今回扱うカメラ連携は、いわゆるマルチモーダル処理の入り口となる。端末のカメラで取得した映像や静止画をモデルに渡し、その内容を言語で説明させたり、質問に答えさせたりする流れだ。Googleの小型モデル「Gemma」系列など、画像を理解できる軽量モデルの広がりにより、視覚と言語を組み合わせた処理が個人の手元でも現実的になりつつある。

一方で、オンデバイス環境特有の難しさも記事では取り上げられているとみられる。クラウド上のAPIと違い、メモリ制約やモデルの読み込み、入力データの前処理など、エラーの原因が多岐にわたるためだ。記事がデバッグを正面から扱う背景には、こうした実装上のハードルを読者と共有する狙いがあると考えられる。

スマートフォンでAI処理を完結させる手法は、通信を介さずに動くことからプライバシー保護やオフライン利用の面で利点が指摘されている。AppleやQualcommなども端末内AIの基盤強化を進めており、ローカルLLMは今後も注目が続く分野といえそうだ。未経験者がAIの助けを借りて開発に挑む本連載は、こうした技術の裾野が着実に広がりつつある状況を象徴しているといえる。
064f783eeb8d3cdf.bodyEn:
The latest installment in a hands-on Zenn series walks through how to add camera input and a debugging workflow to a large language model running entirely on a smartphone. The topic matters because on-device AI is shifting from a research curiosity toward a practical option for everyday developers, and doing it with a phone alone lowers the barrier for newcomers who lack a dedicated GPU or a cloud budget.

The series builds on a previous article that introduced the architecture of the LiteRT-LM engine and its support for text, image, and audio input. LiteRT-LM is part of Google's LiteRT family, the runtime formerly known as TensorFlow Lite that was renamed to reflect its broader role as a lightweight inference engine. LiteRT-LM specifically targets language models, providing the plumbing needed to load quantized weights, manage context, and stream tokens efficiently on resource-constrained hardware.

This new entry focuses on connecting a device camera to the model and on the debugging techniques that make such a project tractable. In practice, camera integration means capturing frames, converting them into the tensor format the model expects, and passing them alongside a text prompt so the model can reason about what it sees. Because multimodal models combine a vision encoder with a language decoder, the image is typically turned into embeddings that share a representation space with text, allowing the model to answer questions about a live scene or a captured photo.

The debugging portion appears aimed at the common friction points of mobile AI development: verifying that input data is preprocessed correctly, confirming that the model loads without exhausting memory, and inspecting latency. On-device inference is unforgiving of mistakes, because errors often surface as silent failures, garbled output, or crashes rather than clear stack traces. The author's emphasis on building with AI assistance also reflects a wider trend in which developers lean on coding assistants to scaffold projects, interpret error messages, and fill knowledge gaps, which is especially helpful for those without prior machine learning experience.

Several factors make this kind of project feasible today. Google's Gemma family, particularly the Gemma 3n variant, was designed for efficient execution on phones and other edge devices, and Google AI Edge tooling, including the MediaPipe LLM Inference API, exposes similar capabilities to application developers. Competing approaches include llama.cpp, MLC LLM, and Ollama on more powerful hardware, while Apple and Qualcomm have invested in dedicated neural accelerators that on-device runtimes can target. Quantization, which reduces model weights to lower precision such as 8-bit or 4-bit integers, is the key technique that lets models with billions of parameters fit within a phone's available memory.

The appeal of running a model locally is consistent across these efforts. Inference happens without sending data to a server, which improves privacy and allows an application to work offline, and it removes per-request API costs. The trade-offs are equally clear: smaller models are less capable than the largest cloud systems, battery and thermal limits constrain sustained use, and memory ceilings cap how much context a model can hold. Camera-driven workloads add their own pressure, since continuously processing frames is more demanding than answering a single text query.

For readers following along, the series positions camera integration as a natural extension of a multimodal pipeline rather than a separate feature, and it frames debugging as an essential skill rather than an afterthought. That framing is sensible, because the gap between a model that merely loads and one that runs reliably tends to be wider on a phone than on a desktop, where memory and tooling are more forgiving.

As mobile tooling matures and phone silicon continues to add AI-specific cores, tutorials like this one suggest that assembling a functional local multimodal assistant is becoming an attainable project rather than a specialist undertaking. Readers without a background in machine learning should still expect to spend time troubleshooting preprocessing, memory, and performance issues, but the combination of a packaged runtime, compact multimodal models, and AI-assisted coding appears to be making the on-device path more approachable than it was even a year ago.

1049e862c636bd43.bodyJa:
ドイツ・ハンブルクで開催中のスーパーコンピューティング国際会議「ISC 2026」で、NVIDIAは科学研究向けのAIを高速化する新しいソフトウェア群を発表した。化学や材料科学における新素材の探索から、宇宙に存在するとされる暗黒物質の探索に至るまで、幅広い科学分野のシミュレーションとデータ解析を加速することを狙ったものだ。

これらのツールはいずれも、同社のGPU向け並列計算基盤であるCUDAをベースに構築されているとみられる。CUDAは画像処理や深層学習だけでなく、近年は高性能計算（HPC）の領域でも事実上の標準的な開発環境として広く使われている。科学計算では従来、物理法則に基づく数値シミュレーションが膨大な計算資源を必要としてきたが、ここにAIによる近似や予測を組み合わせることで、計算時間を大幅に短縮できる可能性が指摘されている。

材料科学の分野では、原子や分子レベルの挙動を扱う第一原理計算や分子動力学が代表的な手法だが、候補物質の組み合わせは膨大で、すべてを実験や精密計算で検証するのは現実的ではない。AIモデルで有望な候補を絞り込み、シミュレーションと組み合わせるアプローチは、電池材料や触媒、半導体など産業応用に直結する領域で注目を集めている。天文学の分野でも、望遠鏡や観測装置が生み出す大量のデータからわずかな信号を抽出する作業に、機械学習が活用され始めている。

NVIDIAはこれまでにも、創薬向けの「BioNeMo」や気候・地球科学向けの「Earth-2」など、特定分野に特化したフレームワークを展開してきた。今回の発表は、こうした科学計算向けソフトウェア戦略をさらに広げる位置づけと考えられる。背景には、生成AIブームによってGPU需要が急増する一方で、研究機関や大学が保有するスーパーコンピュータでもAIと従来型シミュレーションの融合が進んでいる事情がある。

一方で、こうしたツールがどの程度の精度と再現性を実際の研究で示せるかは、今後の検証を待つ必要がある。AIによる予測はあくまで近似であり、物理的な妥当性の確認が欠かせないためだ。また、特定企業のプラットフォームへの依存を懸念する声もあり、オープンな計算基盤との両立が課題となる可能性がある。研究現場での採用が広がれば、科学的発見のスピードを底上げする一助となることが期待される。
1049e862c636bd43.bodyEn:
NVIDIA used the opening of ISC 2026, the International Supercomputing Conference taking place this week in Hamburg, to unveil a collection of software intended to accelerate artificial intelligence for scientific research. The company says the new tools span fields as different as chemistry, materials discovery and the astronomical hunt for dark matter, a breadth that reflects how AI techniques are increasingly being folded into traditional high-performance computing, or HPC.

The releases build on NVIDIA's CUDA platform and its growing catalog of domain-specific libraries and pretrained models. Rather than a single product, the announcement appears to bundle several components targeting distinct stages of the research pipeline, from running large physical simulations to analyzing the enormous datasets that modern instruments and detectors produce. NVIDIA frames this work as "AI for science

b63e2046284c5d9f.bodyJa:
米ロスアラモス国立研究所(LANL)は、ヒューレット・パッカード・エンタープライズ(HPE)およびNVIDIAと共同で、NVIDIAの新型「Vera CPU」を採用した3台のスーパーコンピューター「Mission」「Vision」「Veritas」を構築すると発表した。エージェンティックAI(自律的に計画・実行するAIエージェント)を科学研究に取り入れ、発見の加速を狙う取り組みだ。

Vera CPUは、NVIDIAが次世代データセンター向けに展開する「Vera Rubin」世代の中核を担うプロセッサーと見られる。従来の「Grace CPU」の後継にあたり、Arm系アーキテクチャを基盤に、GPUとの高帯域接続を前提とした設計が特徴とされる。CPUとGPUを密に結合することで、大規模なAIモデルの学習・推論と、物理シミュレーションなどの高性能計算(HPC)を同一基盤で効率的に処理できる点が訴求されている。

注目されるのは「エージェンティックAI」という方向性だ。これは、研究者の指示に単一の回答を返すだけでなく、AI自身が仮説の立案、計算の実行、結果の評価といった一連の作業を半自律的に進める仕組みを指す。LANLはこれにより、材料科学やエネルギー、安全保障に関わる研究などで、人手では時間のかかる探索プロセスを大幅に短縮できる可能性があるとしている。

背景には、米国の主要な国立研究所が相次いで最新のスーパーコンピューターを更新している動きがある。ローレンス・リバモア国立研究所の「El Capitan」やオークリッジ国立研究所の「Frontier」など、エクサスケール級のシステムが稼働するなか、各拠点はAIとHPCの融合を競っている。今回のLANLの計画も、シミュレーション中心だった従来のHPCに生成AIやエージェント技術を組み込む潮流の一例と位置づけられる。

HPEはスーパーコンピューター事業でCray由来の技術を持ち、NVIDIAのGPU・CPUとの組み合わせは近年の大型案件で定番となりつつある。3システムがいつ稼働し、どの程度の規模になるかといった詳細は今後明らかになると見られるが、エージェンティックAIを科学の現場に本格導入する試みとして注目を集めそうだ。
b63e2046284c5d9f.bodyEn:
Los Alamos National Laboratory is preparing to deploy three new supercomputers — named Mission, Vision and Veritas — built in partnership with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and NVIDIA, in what stands as one of the earliest large-scale commitments to NVIDIA's forthcoming Vera CPU. The move matters because it links a next-generation processor to a broader change in how national laboratories intend to pursue research: not simply running ever-larger simulations, but deploying autonomous "agentic" AI systems capable of planning, reasoning and executing multi-step scientific workflows with limited human intervention.

Agentic AI refers to models that go beyond answering a single prompt. Rather than producing one response, an agentic system can break a problem into stages, call external tools, run code, evaluate intermediate results and decide what to do next. In a scientific setting, that could mean an AI agent proposing a hypothesis, configuring a simulation, analyzing the output and refining its approach in successive cycles. Los Alamos appears to be positioning its new machines as platforms where these agents work alongside traditional high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, blending physics-based modeling with machine learning.

The Vera CPU is central to that vision. Vera is NVIDIA's custom Arm-based processor and the successor to the Grace CPU, which the company introduced as the host processor in its Grace Hopper and Grace Blackwell systems. Vera forms half of the Vera Rubin platform, NVIDIA's next architecture, where it is designed to pair tightly with Rubin GPUs over high-bandwidth interconnects. The tight CPU-GPU coupling is intended to reduce data-movement bottlenecks, which are often a limiting factor when feeding large accelerators. For agentic workloads in particular, the CPU handles orchestration, branching logic and the many smaller serial tasks that surround GPU-accelerated computation, so a faster, more capable host processor can meaningfully affect overall throughput.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise is supplying the system design, very likely drawing on its Cray supercomputing lineage. HPE acquired Cray in 2019 and has since built many of the world's largest machines, including exascale systems such as Frontier and El Capitan, the latter housed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. HPE's Slingshot interconnect and liquid-cooled cabinet designs have become common building blocks for Department of Energy supercomputers, and the Mission, Vision and Veritas systems appear to follow that established pattern of HPE integration paired with NVIDIA silicon.

The context for Los Alamos itself is important. The laboratory is one of the U.S. Department of Energy's primary national security sites, with a long history in nuclear weapons stockpile stewardship, materials science and large-scale physics simulation. Because live nuclear testing has been halted for decades, the lab relies heavily on computational modeling to certify and understand its work, making it a consistent early adopter of frontier computing hardware. Extending that mission toward agentic AI suggests the lab sees autonomous systems as a way to accelerate discovery across domains that may include energy research, climate and earth modeling, drug and materials design, and national security applications.

The naming of the three systems hints at distinct roles, though the lab has not publicly detailed exact specifications or how workloads will be partitioned among them. Deploying multiple machines rather than a single flagship can allow a laboratory to separate classified and open research, balance production and experimental work, or stage hardware as it becomes available.

The announcement also fits a wider industry trend. NVIDIA has steadily moved from selling discrete GPUs toward offering full CPU-GPU platforms, and its Arm-based CPUs represent a direct challenge to x86 incumbents Intel and AMD in the data center. At the same time, governments and research institutions are increasingly framing AI not as a standalone tool but as an active participant in the scientific method. Whether agentic systems can reliably deliver trustworthy results in high-stakes scientific environments remains an open question, and such systems are likely to require careful validation against established physics-based methods.

For now, the Los Alamos collaboration signals confidence in NVIDIA's roadmap well before Vera ships in volume. If the systems perform as intended, they could offer an early indication of how the Vera Rubin generation behaves in production HPC settings and how readily agentic AI can be folded into the demanding, accuracy-sensitive work of a national laboratory.

f2f6d582016a3f96.bodyJa:
イスラエルの再生可能エネルギー企業Eco Wave Powerが、NVIDIAのAIインフラとデジタルツイン技術を活用し、波のエネルギーを電力へ変換するシステムの最適化に取り組んでいることが明らかになった。急拡大するAI向け電力需要への対応策として、海洋エネルギーの実用化を後押しする動きとして注目される。

波力発電は、防波堤や桟橋に設置したフロート(浮き)が波の上下動を受けてアームを動かし、その運動を油圧システムなどを介して発電する仕組みが一般的だ。太陽光や風力に比べてエネルギー密度が高く、夜間や無風時でも発電できる安定性が利点とされる一方、塩害や荒天時の機器破損、波の不規則さに合わせた制御の難しさといった課題が普及を阻んできた。

Eco Wave Powerは、こうした複雑な海洋環境をデジタルツインとして仮想空間上に再現し、波の挙動や装置の応答をシミュレーションすることで、発電効率の向上や保守の最適化を図ると見られる。NVIDIAのGPUによる高速演算とAIモデルを組み合わせれば、波の状態をリアルタイムで予測し、フロートの動きを最適に制御できる可能性がある。

背景にあるのは、生成AIや産業用AI、エッジコンピューティングの拡大に伴う電力消費の急増だ。NVIDIAは「次世代のAIは演算能力だけでなくエネルギーによって規定される」との見方を示しており、AIデータセンターを支える電源確保が業界共通の課題となっている。実際、各社はAIの電力需要を見据え、原子力や再生可能エネルギーへの投資を活発化させている。

波力発電は世界的にはまだ実証段階の技術が多く、商用規模での競争力は今後の検証が必要だ。ただ、AIによる設計・運用の高度化が進めば、これまで活用が難しかった海洋資源を新たな電源として組み込める可能性がある。AIの成長がエネルギー技術の革新を促し、その電力を再びAIが利用するという循環が、今後の重要なテーマになりそうだ。
f2f6d582016a3f96.bodyEn:
The next era of artificial intelligence will not be defined by compute alone; its growth is increasingly tied to the availability of clean, reliable energy. As accelerated computing scales across AI factories, agentic systems, industrial automation and edge deployments, the electricity required to power data centers is becoming one of the central constraints on the industry's expansion. Against that backdrop, Eco Wave Power's collaboration with NVIDIA to apply AI infrastructure and digital twin technology to wave energy generation highlights how renewable sources are being re-examined as potential contributors to the power mix that supports AI.

Eco Wave Power, a company focused on converting the motion of ocean and sea waves into electricity, is using NVIDIA's AI infrastructure and digital twin tools to optimize the design and operation of its systems. Wave energy has long been considered a promising but technically challenging renewable resource. Unlike solar and wind, which have matured into large-scale commercial industries, wave power has struggled with the harsh marine environment, the variability of wave conditions, and the engineering difficulty of building devices that survive years of saltwater exposure while remaining efficient. Simulation and modeling are therefore central to making the technology viable, and this is where digital twins appear to play a significant role.

A digital twin is a virtual replica of a physical system that can be used to simulate, monitor and refine real-world behavior. By building digital twins of its wave energy converters and the surrounding marine conditions, Eco Wave Power can test different configurations, predict how equipment will respond to changing waves, and identify optimizations before committing to costly physical hardware. NVIDIA's Omniverse platform, which is designed for building physically based digital twins, and its broader simulation and accelerated computing stack are the kinds of tools typically used for such workloads. The approach is likely intended to shorten development cycles, reduce risk, and improve the energy yield of installations.

The stated motivation behind the effort is the rapidly growing electricity demand driven by AI. Training and running large models requires substantial power, and operators of AI factories and data centers are searching for additional generation capacity, including renewable sources that can help offset the carbon footprint of computing. Wave energy is positioned as a complementary option, particularly for coastal regions, though it remains a small and emerging segment compared with established renewables. It would be premature to suggest that wave power will meet a large share of AI energy needs in the near term; rather, the collaboration appears to be an early example of how AI tooling can be applied to accelerate a still-developing clean energy technology.

This work fits into a wider pattern of NVIDIA promoting its platforms for energy and industrial applications. The company has positioned its accelerated computing, simulation and AI software across sectors such as power grid management, climate modeling and manufacturing, often framing energy efficiency and digital twins as central themes. Related industry moves include growing interest from hyperscale data center operators in securing dedicated renewable and even nuclear power, as well as the use of AI to forecast generation and balance loads on electrical grids. Digital twin technology in particular has gained traction across utilities and heavy industry as a way to model complex physical assets without disrupting live operations.

For Eco Wave Power, the partnership offers access to computing resources and modeling capabilities that smaller renewable developers may otherwise find difficult to assemble. For NVIDIA, the project serves as a demonstration of how its infrastructure can be applied beyond traditional data center workloads to physical and industrial AI, a category the company has emphasized in its recent messaging. The framing also reflects a broader narrative within the industry that compute and energy are becoming intertwined, with the expansion of AI both increasing power demand and providing tools to make energy systems more efficient.

The practical impact of the collaboration will depend on how the optimized systems perform in real deployments and whether wave energy can scale economically. Many wave power projects have historically faced cost and reliability hurdles, so independent results over time will be needed to assess the benefits. Even so, the announcement underscores a notable theme for the years ahead: the convergence of AI, simulation and renewable energy as the demands of computing reshape how the technology sector thinks about power.

2b521c0a98022d91.bodyJa:
AIにコードを書かせる開発が普及するなか、効率の裏で見落とされがちな「設計の劣化」を実体験として記したブログ記事が注目を集めている。Zennに投稿されたこの記事は、AI統合型エディタ「Cursor」を使い始めて約1カ月後に、コードベース全体の設計が崩壊していたという気づきをつづったものだ。

Cursorは、Visual Studio Codeをベースに大規模言語モデル(LLM)を組み込んだエディタで、自然言語による指示でコードの生成や修正、リファクタリングを行える。筆者は当初、「指示を出すたびに画面が完成に近づく」体験に手応えを感じ、コードを自力で書けなくても動くものが作れたと振り返る。こうした即効性は、AI支援開発の最大の魅力とされる。

しかし記事が問題視するのは、短期的な生産性の高さが、長期的な保守性を犠牲にしうる点だ。AIは目の前の指示を満たすコードを次々に出力するが、プロジェクト全体の構造や責務の分担、命名規則の一貫性までを常に踏まえているとは限らない。結果として、似た処理が各所に重複したり、依存関係が複雑に絡み合ったりして、いわゆる技術的負債が蓄積していく可能性がある。

背景には、AIに任せきりにすることで、開発者が設計判断を行う機会を失いやすいという構造がある。どのファイルに何を置き、どこで責務を分けるかといった意思決定を都度AIに委ねると、全体を俯瞰する視点が育ちにくい。動くコードが手早く得られるほど、その傾向は強まると見られる。

同様の課題は、GitHub CopilotやClineといった他のAIコーディング支援ツールでも指摘されてきた。各社は、コードベース全体を文脈として読み込む機能や、設計方針を明文化したルールファイルを参照させる仕組みを整えつつある。Cursorにもプロジェクト固有の指示を与える設定があり、こうした機能の活用が劣化の抑制に寄与するとされる。

この記事が示すのは、AIを使うこと自体の是非ではなく、使い方への問いだろう。生成されたコードを鵜呑みにせず、設計レビューやリファクタリングを人間が主導する姿勢が、持続可能な開発には欠かせないと言えそうだ。
2b521c0a98022d91.bodyEn:
A recent blog post on Zenn describes a developer's experience using Cursor, the AI-assisted code editor, and discovering that the project's architecture had quietly deteriorated over the course of a month. The account is a useful illustration of a problem that is becoming more common as natural-language coding tools lower the barrier to building software: rapid output does not guarantee a maintainable design.

The author's story follows a familiar arc. Cursor lets users describe what they want in plain language, and the tool generates or edits code accordingly. At first, the experience felt almost effortless. Each instruction moved the application closer to completion, and even someone who could not write code by hand was able to produce something that actually ran. The trouble surfaced later, when the accumulated changes had produced a codebase that was difficult to understand, extend, or reason about.

This pattern, sometimes described informally as "vibe coding," reflects a structural tension in AI-assisted development. Large language models are good at producing code that satisfies an immediate request, but they do not inherently maintain a consistent architecture across many such requests. Without a guiding plan, each prompt tends to be answered locally, and the resulting files can drift toward duplication, inconsistent naming, tangled dependencies, and unclear boundaries between components. The individual pieces work, but the whole becomes fragile, which is a textbook description of accumulating technical debt.

Several factors appear to accelerate this decay. When a developer cannot read the generated code closely, they lose the ability to catch design problems early. The model also has a limited view of the project: it works from the context it is given, which may not include the full picture of how modules are supposed to fit together. As a file or function grows, the AI's edits can become less reliable, and a user who is unsure what the code does may accept changes that introduce subtle regressions. Speed, in other words, can mask a slow loss of control.

Cursor, built on a fork of Visual Studio Code by Anysphere, is one of several tools competing in this space. GitHub Copilot popularized inline AI suggestions, while newer agentic tools such as Claude Code, Windsurf, and various IDE integrations push further toward letting the model plan and execute multi-step changes. The capabilities differ, but the underlying caution is the same: the more autonomy a tool has, the more important it becomes to give it structure and to review its output.

The lessons that emerge from accounts like this one are largely a restatement of established software engineering practice, now applied to AI workflows. Defining the architecture before generating code, keeping functions and files small, writing tests, and reviewing changes in small increments all help the human stay in control. Some developers maintain explicit specification or rules files; Cursor supports project rules that shape how the model behaves, which can encode conventions the AI should follow. Breaking work into clearly scoped tasks, rather than requesting sweeping changes, also tends to produce more coherent results.

The broader point is that AI tools shift, rather than remove, the need for engineering judgment. Generating code becomes cheap, so the bottleneck moves to understanding, structuring, and maintaining it. For people learning to program, this creates a particular risk: it is possible to ship a working prototype without ever building the mental model required to maintain it. The author's experience suggests that treating the AI as a fast but unsupervised contributor is likely to end in exactly the kind of design collapse the title describes.

None of this argues against using Cursor or similar tools, which can meaningfully speed up development. It does suggest that their benefits are best realized when paired with deliberate design decisions and consistent review, practices that remain a human responsibility regardless of how much of the typing the model takes over.

f5caf789bb3b9b31.bodyJa:
AIエージェントを使った開発で、特定の機能に手を入れるたびに、過去に直したはずの不具合が再発する。こうした「デグレ(デグレード)」に悩まされる開発者は少なくない。Zennに投稿された「AIが繰り返すデグレをなんとかしたい件」は、Cursorなどのコーディングエージェントを使う中で繰り返し生じるデグレと、その対処の試みを記した実践的な記録だ。なお筆者によれば、本文の約7割はAI自身が書いているという。

記事の発端は、在庫まわりのロジックである。リファクタリングのたびに同じ箇所が壊れ、修正しても別の作業で再び元に戻ってしまう。AIエージェントは指示された範囲のコードは生成できても、プロジェクト全体の文脈や過去の修正意図を完全には保持していないため、こうした再発が起きやすいと見られる。

背景には、現在の大規模言語モデル(LLM)を用いたコード生成の構造的な制約がある。エージェントはコンテキストウィンドウに収まる範囲の情報をもとに推論するため、長大なコードベースや複雑な依存関係の全体像を常に把握しているわけではない。結果として、一度修正したエッジケースが、別のセッションや別の指示のもとで再び見落とされる可能性がある。

こうした課題への対処として、一般的にはテストコードの整備が有効とされる。リグレッションテストや自動テストを用意しておけば、デグレが起きた際に早期に検知できる。加えて、CursorのRulesやAGENTS.mdのような指示ファイルに「壊してはならない仕様」を明文化し、エージェントに繰り返し参照させる手法も広がりつつある。修正の意図をコメントやドキュメントとして残すことも、再発防止の一助になると考えられる。

AIによるコード生成は生産性を高める一方で、品質の担保は人間側の設計に依存する部分が大きい。GitHub CopilotやClaude Codeなど各種エージェントの普及が進むなか、AIの出力をどう検証し、知識をどう蓄積するかは多くの開発現場に共通する論点だ。本記事は、その実務的な悩みと工夫を共有する一例として参考になるだろう。
f5caf789bb3b9b31.bodyEn:
Anyone building software with AI coding agents has probably run into the same frustration: you ask the assistant to adjust one feature, and something that used to work quietly breaks. This phenomenon, known in Japanese developer slang as "degure" (a contraction of the English word "degrade," meaning a regression), is the subject of a recent Zenn post that recounts a developer's struggle with inventory-related logic that kept failing after each round of refactoring. The author is openly candid that roughly 70 percent of the article itself was written by AI, which lends an interesting reflexive quality to its examination of where AI assistance falls short.

Regressions are not new to software engineering, but agentic development appears to amplify them. When a human edits a codebase, they usually carry a mental model of which parts are coupled and which invariants must hold. An AI agent, by contrast, operates within a limited context window and frequently sees only the files it has been handed or has chosen to read. If a change to inventory logic depends on assumptions buried in another module the agent never opened, the model can confidently produce code that satisfies the immediate request while quietly violating an unstated constraint elsewhere. The result is a fix that looks correct in isolation but reintroduces a bug that was solved weeks earlier.

Part of the difficulty is that large language models optimize for plausible, locally coherent output rather than global correctness. They do not inherently "remember" prior fixes unless that history is present in their context or encoded somewhere they can retrieve it. This is why the same class of bug can resurface repeatedly: each session may start with a blank slate, and the agent rediscovers, then re-breaks, the same fragile area. Tightly coupled code, implicit business rules, and sparse documentation all make this worse, because the conditions the agent needs to respect are never made explicit.

The mitigation strategies that tend to come up address exactly these gaps. Automated tests, and regression tests in particular, act as a guardrail that catches breakage the moment it happens rather than after it reaches production; pairing an agent with a solid test suite lets the model iterate against concrete feedback instead of guessing. Keeping changes small and scoped reduces the blast radius of any single edit, and writing down domain rules in a place the agent will actually read helps preserve hard-won knowledge across sessions. In Cursor specifically, project rules files such as .cursorrules or the newer rules format are intended for this purpose, letting teams encode conventions, constraints, and warnings about brittle areas so the assistant carries them into every interaction.

Context management is the broader theme underneath these tactics. Tools increasingly lean on retrieval-augmented generation, codebase indexing, and explicit file referencing to give the model a more complete view before it writes anything. Cursor indexes a repository to improve the relevance of what it retrieves, and competing environments such as GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Anthropic's Claude Code, and the open-source Aider take broadly similar approaches, differing mainly in how aggressively they pull in surrounding context and how much they automate multi-file edits. None of these fully solves the regression problem, but they reduce the chance that an agent acts on a partial picture.

It is worth being measured about what any of this guarantees. Tests only protect the behavior they actually cover, so untested edge cases remain exposed, and rules files help only when they are accurate and maintained. Human review still appears to be the most reliable backstop, especially for code touching critical paths like inventory, billing, or authentication, where a silent regression carries real cost. Treating the agent as a fast but forgetful collaborator, rather than an autonomous engineer, aligns expectations with current capabilities.

The wider context is that AI-assisted development has moved quickly from autocomplete to multi-step agents that can plan, edit several files, and run commands. That power raises the stakes of regressions, because an agent can now change more in a single pass than a developer might review carefully. The Zenn author's experience is a useful reminder that productivity gains from these tools are real but conditional: they depend on the surrounding engineering discipline, including tests, clear constraints, and version control hygiene. For teams adopting agentic workflows, the lesson is less about distrusting the AI and more about building the scaffolding that lets it fail safely.

ec6a71dc524d921a.bodyJa:
Googleが新たに公開したオープンモデル「Gemma 4」が、Ollama経由でローカル環境でも手軽に試せるようになった。本記事で取り上げる検証は、RTX 4070（VRAM 12GB）という一般的なミドルレンジGPU上で、12B・E4B・26Bの3バリアントを含む計5モデルを同一条件で実測したもので、ローカルLLMを選ぶ際の実用的な判断材料として注目される。

検証では、Gemma 4シリーズに加え、Alibabaが手がけるQwen3、Microsoftが開発するPhi-4を同じプロンプトで動かし、推論速度（トークン毎秒）、VRAM消費量、回答の正解性という3つの観点から比較している。ハードウェアと条件をそろえることで、モデル間の素の性能差を見やすくしている点が特徴だ。

ここで前提となるのが、モデルサイズとVRAMの関係である。一般に12GBのVRAMでは、量子化（重みを低ビットに圧縮する手法）を施さないと大きなモデルは載りきらない。26Bのような比較的大きなモデルを動かす場合、4ビット前後の量子化や一部レイヤーのCPUオフロードが必要になり、その分だけ速度が犠牲になる可能性がある。一方でE4Bのような軽量志向のモデルは、省メモリで高速に動く代わりに、複雑なタスクで精度が落ちる傾向があるとされる。

こうしたトレードオフは、ローカルLLMを実用に組み込むうえで避けて通れない論点だ。クラウドAPIと違い、手元のGPUで動かす場合はVRAMの上限が明確な制約になるため、「どのサイズのモデルが自分の環境で現実的に動き、かつ十分な品質を保てるか」を見極める必要がある。Ollamaやllama.cppといったツールの普及で導入の敷居は下がったものの、最適な構成は用途やハードウェアによって変わる。

今回のような同一条件のベンチマークは、カタログスペックだけでは見えにくい実環境での挙動を把握する手がかりになる。ただし結果は特定のGPUやプロンプト、量子化設定に依存するため、自分の用途に近いタスクで追試することが望ましいだろう。オープンモデルの競争が激化するなか、こうした実測情報の価値は今後も高まっていくと見られる。
ec6a71dc524d921a.bodyEn:
Google's Gemma 4 release has reignited a familiar question for anyone running language models locally: how do the new weights behave on a mainstream consumer GPU rather than a data-center accelerator? A recent hands-on report tackles this directly, putting three Gemma 4 variants on an RTX 4070 with 12GB of VRAM and comparing them against Qwen3 and Phi-4 under the same prompts and settings. The focus is practical—generation speed, memory footprint, and correctness—rather than headline leaderboard scores.

The test centers on five models run through Ollama, the widely used local-inference front end built on llama.cpp and the GGUF format. The Gemma 4 lineup under examination spans a 12B dense model, a 26B model, and an "E4B" variant. The E4B naming likely follows the convention introduced with earlier Gemma generations, where the letter denotes an effective parameter count achieved through techniques such as selective parameter activation and per-layer embeddings, so the model behaves like a roughly 4B-class network while drawing on a larger underlying structure. Qwen3, Alibaba's open model family, and Microsoft's Phi-4 round out the comparison as established reference points in the small-to-mid-size open model space.

The 12GB VRAM ceiling is the central constraint shaping the results. A 12B model at 4-bit quantization typically fits comfortably within that budget, leaving room for context, while a 26B model generally cannot reside entirely in 12GB at usable quantization levels. In that situation Ollama offloads the overflow layers to system RAM and the CPU, which preserves the ability to run the model but tends to reduce tokens-per-second throughput substantially. This is why a side-by-side measurement matters: the largest model is not automatically the most useful one on this hardware, because the speed penalty from partial offloading can outweigh modest gains in answer quality for everyday tasks.

Quantization is the prerequisite concept that ties the comparison together. To fit large weights into limited memory, models are compressed to lower numerical precision, commonly 4-bit variants, which trades a degree of accuracy for a smaller footprint and faster inference. Because the report runs each model under matched conditions, it offers a more apples-to-apples view than comparing vendor-published benchmarks that may use different quantization, context lengths, or sampling parameters. Readers should still treat any single accuracy figure cautiously, since results on a small custom test set can be sensitive to prompt phrasing and the specific quantization build used.

For context, the broader trend here is the steady push to make capable models usable without cloud APIs. Local execution appeals to users who want data privacy, predictable cost, and offline availability, and the tooling has matured accordingly. Ollama, LM Studio, and text-generation-webui have lowered the barrier to pulling and running quantized weights, while GGUF has become a de facto distribution format for CPU-and-GPU hybrid inference. The competitive backdrop is equally relevant: Google's Gemma, Alibaba's Qwen, Microsoft's Phi, and Meta's Llama families now iterate on overlapping release cycles, each trying to push more capability into smaller, more efficient packages that suit consumer hardware.

The value of a test like this is in surfacing the trade-offs that aggregate benchmarks tend to hide. An efficient variant such as E4B is likely to deliver the highest throughput and the smallest memory use, making it attractive for interactive or batch workloads where responsiveness matters, while the 12B model appears positioned as the balanced default that fits 12GB without offloading. The 26B model represents the quality-versus-speed extreme, where output may improve but the latency cost on this GPU could be significant. How Qwen3 and Phi-4 slot into that spectrum gives a sense of whether Gemma 4 meaningfully advances the efficiency frontier or merely matches existing options.

Anyone planning to reproduce these measurements should keep a few caveats in mind. Tokens-per-second varies with driver versions, context length, batch size, and background GPU load, and accuracy depends heavily on the evaluation prompts chosen. The figures from one RTX 4070 should be read as directional guidance for similar 12GB cards rather than definitive scores. Even so, this kind of grounded, same-conditions comparison is precisely what helps local-LLM users decide which model to actually download, and it is a useful complement to the official model cards that rarely reflect the realities of a single consumer graphics card.

2dc5fc93a02eecad.bodyJa:
NVIDIAは、大規模なAI処理向けの最新サーバーで、最大45°Cという高温の冷却液で動作できる液体冷却技術を導入したと明らかにした。これは多くの人が15分ほどしか浸かっていられない38〜40°Cのジャグジーより熱く、AIデータセンターの冷却効率と省エネ性能を高める狙いがある。

近年、生成AIの普及で需要が急増したGPUは、世代を追うごとに消費電力と発熱量が増している。NVIDIAのGrace Blackwellに代表されるラックスケールのAIシステムでは、1ラックあたりの電力密度が従来型サーバーをはるかに上回り、空気だけで冷やすのは難しくなった。そこで主流になりつつあるのが、チップに直接冷却液を接触させる「ダイレクト・トゥ・チップ」方式などの液体冷却だ。

今回のポイントは、冷却液の温度を高く保ったまま運用できる点にある。一般に冷却液を低温に保つには、冷凍機（チラー）で電力を消費して冷やす必要がある。だが45°Cという高い温度でも十分に冷却できるなら、外気や乾式クーラーを利用する「フリークーリング」の比率を高め、チラーの稼働を減らせる可能性がある。結果として、データセンター全体の消費電力やPUE（電力使用効率）の改善、さらには冷却に使う水の削減につながると見られる。

こうした高温水冷却の流れは、AIインフラ全体が抱える課題と直結している。膨大な電力を消費する「AIファクトリー」の運用コストや環境負荷をいかに抑えるかは、クラウド各社や半導体業界に共通するテーマだ。マイクロソフトやグーグルといったハイパースケーラーも液浸冷却や水冷の採用を進めており、冷却技術は演算性能と同じくらい重要な競争軸になりつつある。

排熱を高温で取り出せることには副次的な利点もある。回収した熱を地域暖房などに再利用する取り組みは欧州を中心に広がっており、温度が高いほど再利用しやすいとされる。AIの計算需要が拡大を続けるなか、今回の刷新は、冷却を性能・コスト・持続可能性の三つを左右する重要技術と位置づける動きの一例と言えそうだ。
2dc5fc93a02eecad.bodyEn:
NVIDIA has detailed an update to the liquid cooling approach used in its latest AI servers, saying its newest systems can operate with coolant supplied at temperatures as high as 45 degrees Celsius. That number matters because it is warmer than a typical hot tub, which sits around 38 to 40 degrees and is hot enough that most people can only soak for about 15 minutes. More importantly, warmer coolant can—counterintuitively—make a data center significantly more energy efficient.

The logic rests on how data centers reject heat. The heat absorbed by the coolant must eventually be released to the outside environment, and when servers demand cold water, operators typically rely on mechanical chillers, essentially large refrigeration units that consume substantial electricity. If chips can be kept within safe limits using warmer liquid, a facility can lean more heavily on so-called free cooling, using outside air, dry coolers, or cooling towers without running power-hungry compressors. In many climates this allows chillers to be downsized or avoided for much of the year, cutting both energy use and water consumption.

NVIDIA's high-density systems use direct-to-chip liquid cooling, in which coolant flows through cold plates mounted directly on the hottest components, principally the GPUs and CPUs. Coolant distribution units, or CDUs, circulate the liquid between the racks and the facility's water loop. Raising the acceptable inlet temperature to 45 degrees widens the gap between the coolant and the outside air across more hours and more locations, which is what enables the efficiency gains. It also serves another goal: the warmer the water leaving the racks, the more useful that waste heat becomes for reuse, such as district heating.

The shift is being driven by the rising power density of AI hardware. NVIDIA refers to large AI installations as "AI factories," and its rack-scale platforms such as the GB200 NVL72 concentrate dozens of GPUs into a single rack, pushing power draw well beyond what air cooling can practically handle. Air-cooled racks have historically operated in the range of a few kilowatts to perhaps 20 or 30 kilowatts; modern accelerated racks are reaching past 100 kilowatts, and future generations are expected to climb higher still. At those densities, liquid cooling moves from optional to effectively required, because liquids carry heat away far more efficiently than air.

The broader industry has been moving in the same direction. Hyperscale operators including Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon have been deploying or testing liquid cooling for AI clusters, and standards bodies such as ASHRAE have published thermal guidelines for warm-water cooling that classify operating ranges by temperature. Some operators are also exploring immersion cooling, where entire boards are submerged in dielectric fluid, though direct-to-chip designs currently appear to be the more common path for large GPU deployments because they integrate more readily with existing rack and facility infrastructure.

A common way to measure this efficiency is power usage effectiveness, or PUE, the ratio of total facility energy to the energy delivered to the computing equipment. Reducing the energy spent on chillers and pumps pushes PUE toward the ideal value of 1.0. NVIDIA frames the 45-degree capability as a way to help operators cut cooling overhead and, in suitable climates, reduce reliance on water—an increasingly sensitive issue as data centers expand and face scrutiny over local resource use.

As with any vendor disclosure, the headline figure represents a capability rather than a guaranteed outcome. Actual savings will depend on local climate, facility design, and how aggressively operators tune their systems. Running components at higher coolant temperatures also leaves less thermal margin, so engineering the cold plates, flow rates, and control logic to stay within safe limits is essential. Even so, the direction is clear: as AI workloads push rack power ever higher, the ability to cool chips with warmer liquid is likely to become a meaningful lever for controlling the energy and water footprint of large AI data centers, and a competitive consideration for the operators building them.

e4cdd2bbf0ad0d50.bodyJa:
スマートフォンの処理性能が年々向上したことで、ChatGPTやGeminiのようなクラウドサービスに接続せず、端末内だけで生成AIを動かす「ローカルLLM」が現実的な選択肢になりつつある。今回取り上げる記事は、プログラミング未経験者でもスマホ単体でチャットボットを構築する手順を、基本から解説するものだ。

ローカルLLMが注目される背景には、スマホに搭載されるSoC（System on Chip）の進化がある。近年のチップはCPUやGPUに加え、AI処理に特化したNPU（ニューラル処理ユニット）を備え、比較的小規模な言語モデルであれば端末上で推論を実行できるようになった。クラウドを介さないため通信が不要でオフラインでも動作し、入力した内容が外部サーバーに送られない点もプライバシー面の利点とされる。

技術的な鍵となるのが「量子化」と呼ばれる軽量化手法だ。モデルの数値表現の精度を落としてファイルサイズと必要メモリを削減することで、数十億パラメータ規模のモデルでもスマホで扱える可能性が出てくる。MetaのLlama 3.2やGoogleのGemma、MicrosoftのPhi、AlibabaのQwenなど、数B（十億）パラメータ前後の小型モデルが相次いで公開されており、こうした流れが個人での実装を後押ししている。

実際に動かすための周辺ツールも整いつつある。Androidでは「Termux」上でllama.cppを動かす方法や、「MLC LLM」「PocketPal」といったアプリが知られ、iOSでも端末内で完結するアプリが登場している。多くの場合、GGUF形式などに変換されたモデルファイルを読み込ませる構成が一般的だ。

一方で、スマホ単体での実行には限界もある。メモリや発熱の制約から動かせるモデルの規模は限られ、応答速度や回答精度はクラウドの大規模モデルに及ばない場面が多いと見られる。それでも、AppleのApple IntelligenceやGoogleのGemini Nanoなど、端末内AIを前提とした機能を主要メーカーが推進しており、オンデバイスAIは今後さらに身近になる可能性がある。本記事は、その第一歩を自分の手で体験するための入門として位置づけられる。
e4cdd2bbf0ad0d50.bodyEn:
Running a large language model entirely on a smartphone, with no cloud connection and no API fees, has shifted from a curiosity to a practical option over the past few years. As mobile systems-on-chip (SoCs) have grown more capable, the idea of a "local LLM" that completes every inference step inside the handset itself has become realistic. This guide-style piece frames that shift for beginners, walking through why on-device models matter and how someone with no prior experience can assemble a basic chat application by working alongside AI tools.

The core appeal is straightforward. When a model runs locally, prompts and responses never leave the device, which addresses a common privacy concern with services such as ChatGPT or Gemini that send text to remote servers. Local inference also works offline, removes per-token usage costs, and can reduce latency for short exchanges. These trade-offs come at the price of raw capability: a model small enough to fit in a phone's memory cannot match the largest cloud systems. For many everyday tasks, however, the gap appears to be narrowing as smaller models improve.

The technical enabler is a combination of hardware and software progress. Modern smartphone SoCs from vendors like Qualcomm, MediaTek, and Apple now include neural processing units (NPUs) alongside multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and they ship with several gigabytes of unified memory. On the software side, quantization is the key technique that makes this feasible. By reducing the numerical precision of a model's weights from 16-bit floating point down to 4-bit or 8-bit integers, quantization can shrink a model's footprint by roughly two-thirds to three-quarters with only modest quality loss. A model with one to three billion parameters, quantized to four bits, can occupy well under two gigabytes, which is within reach of a mid-range to high-end phone.

The most common foundation for this work is llama.cpp, an open-source C++ inference engine optimized for consumer hardware. It popularized the GGUF file format, now a de facto standard for distributing quantized models. On Android, many enthusiasts run llama.cpp through Termux, a terminal emulator that provides a Linux-like environment without rooting the device. Others prefer purpose-built apps. PocketPal and ChatterUI on Android, and several MLC LLM-based applications on both Android and iOS, let users download a model and start chatting through a graphical interface. MLC LLM, a separate project, compiles models to run efficiently across diverse hardware backends, including mobile GPUs.

Choosing a model is the next step, and the field has expanded quickly. Compact, capable options include Meta's Llama 3.2 in 1-billion and 3-billion parameter sizes, Google's Gemma 2B, Microsoft's Phi-3 Mini, and Alibaba's Qwen series, several of which are released with open weights specifically to encourage local deployment. These smaller models are often described as suitable for summarization, drafting, simple question answering, and casual conversation, while more demanding reasoning or coding tasks may still favor larger cloud models.

The "basic chat construction" focus of this edition reflects a sensible starting point. A minimal chat loop requires loading the model, formatting user input with the correct prompt or chat template, running inference, and streaming the generated tokens back to the screen. Each model family expects a particular template, and mismatches are a frequent cause of garbled or unhelpful output, so following the model card's instructions matters. Building this with AI assistance—using a chatbot to explain commands, debug errors, and suggest code—is itself part of the article's premise, lowering the barrier for newcomers.

It is worth setting expectations around performance and constraints. Generation speed on a phone is typically measured in a handful of tokens per second, sustained inference can warm the device and drain the battery, and available memory limits how large a model and how long a context window can be. These limits are the reason small, quantized models dominate the mobile space rather than the multi-billion-parameter systems used in data centers.

The broader context is an industry-wide push toward on-device AI. Apple Intelligence, Google's Gemini Nano within the AICore framework, and Samsung's Galaxy AI all point to a future where some inference happens locally by default. Hobbyist projects and these vendor efforts are likely to converge, making private, offline assistants an increasingly normal feature rather than an experiment.

de5ad191793f283b.bodyJa:
AIコーディングエージェントを対話的に使うのは便利だが、同じ作業を繰り返すなら、その都度プロンプトを打ち込むのは煩わしい。Cognition社が提供する「Devin for Terminal」、すなわち `devin` コマンドには、対話を介さずに一度の指示で処理を完結させる非対話モードが用意されており、シェルスクリプトやCIパイプラインへの組み込みに適している。

`devin -p` の `-p` は print（出力）を意味するとみられ、プロンプトを引数として渡すと、エージェントがタスクを実行して結果を標準出力に返す。対話セッションのように入力待ちで止まらないため、パイプやリダイレクトと組み合わせて結果を別ファイルに保存したり、後続のコマンドへ渡したりできる。この発想は、Anthropicの「Claude Code」が備える同名の `-p`（`--print`）オプションと共通しており、ターミナルベースのAIエージェントが揃って「対話」と「バッチ実行」の二つの顔を持ちつつある流れを反映している可能性がある。

非対話モードが効くのは、人手を介さず繰り返したい定型処理だ。たとえばコミットメッセージの自動生成、プルリクエストの差分要約、テスト失敗ログの一次解析といったタスクを、Gitフックやcronジョブから呼び出せる。前回紹介されたSkills、Subagents、Hooks、`/handoff` といった機能が対話の中で力を発揮するのに対し、`-p` はそれらを定型フローへ落とし込むための入り口になり得る。

ただし、自動実行には注意も伴う。エージェントにファイルの書き換えやコマンド実行をどこまで許可するかは、スクリプト化すると人間の確認が挟まりにくくなる。実行範囲の制限やドライラン、出力のログ保存といった安全策を併用するのが無難だろう。また、大規模言語モデルの応答は実行ごとに揺れる可能性があるため、結果をそのまま本番へ流すのではなく、検証ステップを挟む設計が現実的だ。

対話に疲れたと感じても、すべてを手動でこなす必要はない。`devin -p` を起点に、AIエージェントを既存のツールチェーンの一部として組み込む——そうした使い方が、今後の開発現場で標準的な選択肢になっていく可能性がある。
de5ad191793f283b.bodyEn:
Devin for Terminal, the command-line agent from Cognition, is most often used the way its name suggests: you open a shell, type devin, and hold a back-and-forth conversation while the agent reads files, runs commands, and edits code. That interactive loop is convenient for exploration, but it becomes a bottleneck the moment you want the same agent to run unattended. The non-interactive mode invoked with devin -p is built for exactly that situation, letting you pass a single prompt and embed the agent inside scripts, pipelines, and scheduled jobs rather than sitting at the keyboard to babysit it.

The pattern will feel familiar to anyone who has used Claude Code, which exposes a comparable print mode through its own -p flag. In both tools the idea is to collapse a multi-turn session into a single request-and-response invocation: you supply the instruction as an argument or over standard input, the agent executes, prints its result to standard output, and exits. Because the command terminates on its own and returns control to the calling process, it can be chained with other commands, redirected to a file, or wrapped in any language that can spawn a subprocess. This is the difference between a tool you operate and a tool you orchestrate.

That distinction matters because it turns an agent into a composable building block. A prompt piped into devin -p can be combined with the rest of the Unix toolset, so the output of one command becomes the input to the agent, and the agent's output flows on to the next stage. Typical applications include cron jobs that summarize the day's commits, git hooks that draft a commit message or review a diff before it lands, and continuous integration steps that triage failing tests or open a draft pull request. Anywhere you already glue tools together with a shell script, the non-interactive agent can slot in as one more stage.

There are a few practical considerations worth planning for. Agentic output is inherently non-deterministic, so a script that depends on a precise string or format should treat the response defensively, ideally requesting structured output and validating it before acting. Permissions are the second concern: an agent that can run arbitrary commands needs explicit boundaries when no human is watching, so it is sensible to scope what it may touch, run it in a sandboxed working directory, and prefer modes that avoid destructive actions unless they are clearly intended. Cost and latency also accumulate quickly when an agent is invoked on every commit or on a tight schedule, which makes it worth limiting how often and on how much input the job actually fires.

It helps to see this within the broader shift among coding agents toward being headless and automatable rather than purely conversational. Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex CLI, Google's Gemini CLI, Aider, and others have all converged on the same insight: developers want both a chat-style interface for thinking through a problem and a quiet batch interface for wiring the same capability into existing automation. The flag conventions differ, and the underlying models and tool integrations vary, but the design goal is shared. Cognition's earlier offering was the cloud-hosted Devin agent that runs as a managed worker; the terminal variant brings a similar agent down to the local machine, and the non-interactive mode extends that reach into the parts of a workflow where a person is not present.

The previous article in this series walked through the interactive features that make the terminal experience pleasant, including Skills, Subagents, Hooks, and the /handoff command, all of which assume someone is steering in real time. The non-interactive mode is the natural complement to those features. Once a task has been validated through hands-on use, expressing it as a devin -p invocation lets you capture that workflow as code, version it alongside the project, and run it repeatedly without the cognitive overhead of a live session. For teams already comfortable with the agent, the payoff is less about new capability and more about reliability and repeatability, which is often what separates a clever demo from something you can depend on day to day.

0f31b1d3f4455ef9.bodyJa:
AI を組み込んだコードエディタ「Cursor」が、開発者それぞれの作業フローに合わせて機能を拡張・調整できるカスタマイズ機能を強化した。プラグイン、スキル、MCP という三つの仕組みを軸に、新設された「Customize」ページから一括で管理できるようになった点が今回の更新の中心だ。

カスタマイズの土台となるのは大きく三つの要素である。プラグインは外部機能を追加してエディタの挙動を拡張する仕組み、スキルは特定の作業手順やノウハウをモデルに与えて繰り返し利用できるようにする仕組みとされる。そして MCP（Model Context Protocol）は、AI モデルが外部のツールやデータソースと接続するためのオープンな規格で、Anthropic が提唱したことで知られる。これらを組み合わせることで、定型的なタスクの自動化や、社内システム・各種 API との連携が進めやすくなると見られる。

これまで Cursor では、こうした拡張設定が複数の画面や設定ファイルに分散しがちだった。新しい「Customize」ページは、プラグイン・スキル・MCP の追加や有効化、無効化を一か所に集約することを狙ったもので、設定の見通しを良くし、チーム内で構成を共有しやすくする効果が期待される。

背景には、AI コーディング支援ツールの競争激化がある。GitHub Copilot や各種 VS Code 拡張、さらに Anthropic の Claude Code など、開発環境に AI を組み込む製品が相次いで登場しており、各社は単なるコード補完にとどまらず、開発者ごとのワークフローへの適応力を競い始めている。MCP のような共通規格への対応は、エコシステム全体の相互運用性を高める動きの一環とも言える。

一方で、外部プラグインや MCP サーバーを通じて多様なツールと接続できるようになるほど、権限管理やセキュリティ、信頼できる提供元の見極めといった運用面の課題も重みを増す。導入にあたっては、利用するスキルやサーバーの出所を確認し、必要な範囲に権限を絞る運用が求められそうだ。Cursor のカスタマイズ機能は、こうした拡張性と管理性の両立をどこまで実現できるかが、今後の評価軸になると考えられる。
0f31b1d3f4455ef9.bodyEn:
Cursor has introduced a consolidated approach to customization that lets developers adapt the AI-assisted code editor to their own workflows through three mechanisms: plugins, skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. According to the changelog, these previously separate capabilities are now gathered behind a single Customize page, a change that matters because it reduces the friction of discovering, configuring, and maintaining the various ways Cursor can be extended. For teams that depend on consistent AI behavior across many projects, a unified surface makes it easier to standardize setups and onboard new contributors.

Cursor is an AI-first editor built as a fork of Visual Studio Code, and much of its appeal comes from how deeply its assistant and agent features integrate with a working codebase. The three customization primitives address different layers of that experience. Plugins extend the editor and its agent with additional functionality. Skills define reusable instructions or specialized capabilities that shape how the AI approaches particular tasks. MCP servers connect Cursor to external tools, data sources, and services. Bringing them together appears intended to give users a clearer mental model of what can be changed and where those settings live.

The Model Context Protocol component is the most industry-relevant of the three. MCP is an open standard originally introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 to provide a common way for AI applications to talk to external systems, such as databases, issue trackers, documentation stores, and internal APIs. Rather than each tool inventing its own bespoke integration format, MCP defines a shared protocol so that a server written once can be reused across compatible clients. Support for MCP has since spread across the AI tooling landscape, and its presence in Cursor's customization page reflects how central the standard has become for connecting coding assistants to real-world context. In practice, this means a developer can point Cursor at an MCP server to let the agent query a project's design system, search internal wikis, or trigger actions in other systems without leaving the editor.

Skills, as a concept, echo a broader trend toward packaging reusable, task-specific guidance for AI agents. The term has been used elsewhere in the industry, including by Anthropic for its Claude models, to describe modular sets of instructions that an agent can load when relevant. In Cursor, skills appear to serve a similar purpose: encapsulating conventions, procedures, or domain knowledge so the assistant behaves predictably for recurring tasks. This is conceptually adjacent to existing Cursor features such as rules files, which let teams encode coding standards and project context that the AI should follow.
