e43af2d606a3f564.bodyEn:
Ollama, one of the most widely used tools for running large language models on local hardware, has published v0.30.7-rc1, a release candidate that centers on a single targeted fix to its OpenAI-compatible API. The change aligns the model list exposed through that compatibility layer with the tags Ollama already tracks internally, resolving the behavior reported in issue #16556. While modest in scope, the update matters to developers who point existing OpenAI client code at a local Ollama instance and expect the returned model inventory to match what is actually installed.

The core of the fix concerns consistency between two views of the same data. Ollama maintains a native endpoint, commonly reached at /api/tags, that lists the models a user has pulled or created, including their tag variants such as different quantizations or parameter sizes. Separately, Ollama offers an OpenAI-compatible surface, typically served under a /v1 path, so that software written for OpenAI's API can talk to a local model with minimal changes. That compatibility includes a models listing endpoint analogous to OpenAI's own. According to the release notes, the OpenAI-compatible list was not fully in step with the tag-based view, and v0.30.7-rc1 reconciles the two so that the names and entries reported through the compatible API correspond to the tags Ollama recognizes.

For application developers, this kind of alignment reduces friction in tooling that enumerates available models before making a request. Many frameworks and user interfaces call a models endpoint to populate a dropdown, validate a requested model name, or route traffic. When the compatible listing diverges from the underlying tags, a model that exists locally may appear missing, or a name returned by the API may not be directly usable in a subsequent completion call. By keeping the two representations synchronized, the release is likely to make automated model discovery more predictable for clients that assume OpenAI-style semantics.

It is worth emphasizing what a release candidate signifies in this context. The "rc1" suffix indicates that the build is intended for testing ahead of a stable v0.30.7 release rather than for general production deployment. Release candidates let maintainers and early adopters verify that a change behaves as intended across platforms and configurations before it is promoted. Users who depend on stability in automated pipelines may prefer to wait for the final tagged version, while those affected by the listed issue can validate the fix early and report any regressions. The narrow changelog, focused on a single issue, suggests this candidate appears to be a maintenance step rather than a feature-bearing update.

Some background helps explain why OpenAI compatibility occupies such a prominent place in Ollama's roadmap. OpenAI's API conventions have become a de facto standard, and a broad ecosystem of libraries, agents, and orchestration layers speaks that dialect. By emulating those endpoints, Ollama lets developers reuse existing code and swap a remote, paid service for a locally hosted model that keeps data on the user's machine. That positioning places Ollama alongside other projects pursuing local or self-hosted inference, including llama.cpp, which underpins much of the local model runtime landscape, as well as LM Studio, GPT4All, and server-oriented systems such as vLLM and text-generation-inference that also expose OpenAI-compatible interfaces. Compatibility quirks like the one addressed here are a recurring theme across these tools, because matching another API's exact contract involves many small behaviors beyond the main request and response shapes.

The wider context is a steady maturation of the local LLM space, where the emphasis has shifted from simply running a model to integrating it cleanly into established developer workflows. Privacy, cost control, offline operation, and the ability to experiment without per-token billing continue to drive interest in on-device inference, and the practical value of these tools often hinges on how faithfully they mirror the cloud APIs that applications already target. Incremental fixes that tighten that fidelity, even ones as small as a corrected model listing, contribute to the reliability that production users expect.

For now, those interested in v0.30.7-rc1 can review the project's release page and issue tracker for the specifics of #16556 and any accompanying notes. Anyone running the candidate should treat it as pre-release software and watch for the stable v0.30.7 build, which is expected to incorporate this fix once testing concludes.

9898e14966f2cdef.bodyJa:
高速エディタとして知られるZed Editorのバージョン1.5.4が、2026年6月6日にリリースされた。今回は新機能の追加よりも既存機能の不具合修正に重点を置いたパッチリリースで、特にdiff表示やエージェント連携まわりの安定性向上が中心となっている。

主要な修正の一つが、サイドバイサイド形式のdiffビューに関するものだ。差分を左右に並べて表示する分割ビューを解除した際に、エディタがクラッシュする問題が報告されていた。コードレビューやバージョン管理の作業で頻繁に使われる機能だけに、この修正は日常的な利用体験に直接影響すると見られる。

もう一つの注目点は、ACP(Agent Client Protocol)レジストリからのエージェントのダウンロードに失敗する不具合の解消だ。ACPはエディタと外部のAIエージェントをつなぐためのプロトコルで、Zedはこの仕組みを通じて多様なAIアシスタントを取り込めるよう設計されている。レジストリからの取得が安定すれば、エージェント機能を活用するユーザーにとって導入のハードルが下がる可能性がある。

加えて、エディタ内の診断ナビゲーションも改善された。診断とは、言語サーバー(LSP)が検出するエラーや警告のことで、これらの箇所をすばやく移動できる機能はコーディング効率に関わる。今回の改善により、問題箇所間の移動がよりスムーズになることが期待される。

Zedは、Atomやtree-sitterの開発に携わったメンバーが中心となって開発するRust製のエディタで、ネイティブな描画性能やマルチプレイヤー編集機能、近年強化が進むAI支援機能を特徴とする。AIを統合したエディタの分野では、MicrosoftのVS Code系拡張やCursorなどが競合として存在し、各社がエージェント機能の取り込みを競い合っている。今回のパッチは派手な変更ではないものの、こうした基盤機能の安定化を地道に積み重ねる開発姿勢がうかがえる。利用中のユーザーは、最新版へ更新することで該当する不具合の影響を回避できる。
9898e14966f2cdef.bodyEn:
Zed has released version 1.5.4 of its code editor, a maintenance update focused on stability rather than new capabilities. Although patch releases rarely command attention, this one matters because it repairs a crash linked to diff handling and restores the editor's ability to download AI agents through its Agent Client Protocol registry, both of which sit at the center of workflows that have grown more important as code review and AI assistance become routine parts of development.

The most disruptive fix addresses a crash that occurred when users unsplit side-by-side diff views. Zed supports a split layout for comparing file changes, placing an original version and a modified version next to each other so differences are easy to scan. Collapsing that layout back into a single pane could previously terminate the editor unexpectedly. For anyone reviewing pull requests or reconciling local Git changes, an abrupt crash can interrupt concentration and risk unsaved context, so eliminating it removes a meaningful source of friction even if the underlying scenario is narrow.

A second fix resolves failures when downloading agents from the ACP Registry. The Agent Client Protocol is an open standard that Zed has been developing to define how editors and external AI coding agents communicate, conceptually similar to how the Language Server Protocol standardized communication between editors and language tooling. The registry appears to serve as a distribution point from which compatible agents can be fetched and installed. When that download path breaks, users are effectively cut off from adding or updating agents, so restoring it is a prerequisite for the broader agent-driven features Zed has been promoting. The presence of this fix suggests the agent ecosystem is still maturing and that the registry mechanics are being actively hardened.

The release also improves diagnostic navigation within the editor. Diagnostics are the errors, warnings, and hints surfaced by language servers as code is written, and navigation refers to moving quickly between them, typically with keyboard shortcuts that jump to the next or previous issue. The changelog does not detail the precise behavior that changed, but smoother movement between diagnostics is the kind of refinement that compounds over a long editing session, helping developers clear a list of problems without manually hunting through a file.

Some context helps explain why these particular fixes appear together. Zed is a high-performance, GPU-accelerated editor written in Rust, developed by Zed Industries, a team that includes contributors behind the earlier Atom editor and the Tree-sitter parsing library. The project positions itself as a fast, collaborative alternative to established tools such as Visual Studio Code, and it has increasingly leaned into native AI integration. That direction places it alongside AI-forward editors like Cursor and Windsurf, as well as assistants such as GitHub Copilot, all of which are competing to embed agents directly into the coding loop rather than treating them as separate chat windows.

The Agent Client Protocol is central to how Zed differentiates that effort. By defining a shared interface, the protocol is intended to let multiple agents, potentially from different providers, plug into the editor without bespoke integration work for each one. This mirrors a wider industry pattern in which open protocols, including the Model Context Protocol popularized for connecting models to external data and tools, aim to reduce lock-in and encourage interoperability. The fix in 1.5.4 is incremental, but it reinforces that Zed treats reliable agent distribution as core infrastructure rather than an experimental add-on.

For existing users, the practical takeaway is straightforward: 1.5.4 is a recommended update for anyone who works heavily with diff views, depends on agents sourced through the ACP Registry, or relies on diagnostics to move through a codebase. Because it is a patch release, it is unlikely to introduce behavioral changes beyond the stated repairs, which lowers the risk of upgrading. As always, users tracking the project closely may wish to consult the official release notes for the complete list of changes, since concise summaries can omit smaller adjustments that affect specific configurations or platforms.

53c01271756be8fe.bodyJa:
ローカルで大規模言語モデル（LLM）を手軽に動かせる人気ツール「Ollama」の最新リリース候補版となる v0.30.7-rc0 が公開された。今回の更新は Windows 環境での起動処理の改善に焦点を当てたもので、安定版に向けた検証用の位置づけとなる。

リリースノートによれば、主な変更点はランチャーが Windows ネイティブの Hermes 設定パスを参照するよう修正された点だ。これにより、Windows ユーザーがアプリケーションを起動する際の構成読み込みの挙動が改善されると見られる。従来は設定ファイルの参照先が環境に最適化されておらず、起動時の構成処理で不整合が生じる場合があった可能性があるが、今回の修正でプラットフォーム標準のパスに沿った動作が期待できる。

ここで言う「rc」（リリース候補）とは、正式版の前に不具合の有無を確認するための先行配布版を指す。新機能の追加よりも安定性の検証が主目的であり、本番環境よりも検証目的での利用が想定される。Ollama は近年、機能追加だけでなく Windows や macOS のネイティブアプリ体験の整備を継続的に進めており、今回の修正もその一環と位置づけられる。

Ollama は、Llama や Mistral、Gemma など多様なオープンモデルをコマンド一つで取得・実行できる点が支持を集めている。ローカル実行はクラウド API と比べてデータが外部に送信されにくく、プライバシーやコスト面での利点があるため、開発者や企業の関心が高い分野だ。競合・関連する選択肢としては、GUI を備えた LM Studio や、軽量推論エンジンの llama.cpp、デスクトップ向けの Jan などが挙げられ、ローカル LLM をめぐる環境整備は活発に進んでいる。

Windows でのセットアップに不便を感じていた利用者にとって、今回の起動まわりの改善は地味ながら実用的な意味を持つ。ただし rc 版は正式リリース前のため、重要な用途で利用する際は安定版の登場を待つか、十分な検証を行うことが望ましいだろう。
53c01271756be8fe.bodyEn:
Ollama has published v0.30.7-rc0, a release candidate that focuses on configuration handling for Windows users. While the change set is small, it matters for anyone running local large language models on Windows, where startup reliability and correct configuration discovery are recurring pain points compared with the more mature macOS and Linux paths.

The headline change in this candidate is that the launcher now uses the native Windows Hermes configuration path. In practice this appears to adjust where and how Ollama reads its configuration during startup, aligning the process with platform-native conventions rather than relying on a more generic or cross-platform approach. The stated effect is improved startup behavior on Windows, which typically translates to fewer cases where settings are missed, misread, or applied inconsistently when the application initializes. Because this is a release candidate labeled rc0, it is intended for testing and feedback ahead of a stable v0.30.7, and users should treat it as a preview rather than a production build.

It is worth being precise about what a release candidate signals. The rc0 suffix indicates the first candidate build in a cycle, meaning the maintainers believe the code is close to final but want broader validation before promoting it to a general release. Behavior can still change between rc0 and the eventual stable tag, and additional candidates (rc1, rc2, and so on) may follow if testers surface regressions. For most users who prioritize stability, waiting for the final v0.30.7 is the conservative choice; for those affected by Windows configuration issues, the candidate offers an early opportunity to verify the fix in their own environment.

For readers less familiar with the project, Ollama is an open-source tool that makes it straightforward to download, run, and manage large language models locally. It packages models, weights, and runtime configuration into a single workflow, exposes a command-line interface and a local HTTP API, and supports a catalog of open models such as Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, and Phi, among others. Running models locally keeps data on the user's machine, avoids per-token cloud costs, and enables offline use, which is why the tool has become popular with developers building retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, chat interfaces, and agent prototypes. The trade-off is that local inference depends heavily on available hardware, particularly GPU memory, so configuration correctness and predictable startup are meaningful quality-of-life factors.

Configuration and launcher details like the one in this release candidate are easy to overlook but tend to have an outsized impact on day-to-day usability. On Windows specifically, differences in file path conventions, permissions, and where applications are expected to store settings can cause subtle failures that are hard to diagnose. Aligning Ollama's startup logic with native Windows expectations is the kind of incremental hardening that accumulates into a smoother experience over successive releases, even if no single change is dramatic on its own.

The broader context is a crowded and fast-moving local-LLM ecosystem. Ollama sits alongside alternatives and complementary projects such as llama.cpp, which provides the underlying inference engine many of these tools build upon, as well as LM Studio, Jan, and GPT4All, which offer graphical interfaces for running models on personal hardware. Front-ends like Open WebUI frequently pair with Ollama's API to provide a browser-based chat experience. Improvements to Windows support are notable because Windows remains the most widely used desktop operating system, and a sizable share of developers and enthusiasts experimenting with local models do so on Windows machines.

Users who want to try the candidate can typically obtain it from the project's GitHub releases page, where binaries and detailed changelogs are published for each tag. As always with pre-release software, it is advisable to note the current installed version before upgrading and to be prepared to roll back if unexpected behavior arises. Anyone relying on Ollama in automated workflows or production-adjacent settings is likely better served by the forthcoming stable release, while those troubleshooting Windows startup or configuration problems may find this candidate worth evaluating and reporting back on to help finalize v0.30.7.

789ae57829cd1b90.bodyJa:
LangChainのエコシステムで、PerplexityのAPIを利用するための連携パッケージ「langchain-perplexity」のバージョン1.3.2が公開された。今回はパッチリリースで、ツール呼び出しに関わるメッセージのシリアライズ処理の不具合を修正した点が唯一の変更となる。

具体的には、ToolMessageおよびAIMessage.tool_callsが正しくシリアライズされない問題が解消された。LangChainではモデルとのやり取りをメッセージオブジェクトとして表現しており、ToolMessageはツール実行の結果を、AIMessage.tool_callsはモデルが要求したツール呼び出しの内容を保持する。これらが正しく直列化・復元されないと、エージェントの動作や状態の保存・読み込みに支障が出る可能性がある。

シリアライズは、会話履歴やエージェントの状態を保存して再利用したり、ネットワーク越しにデータをやり取りしたりする際の基礎となる処理である。特にツール呼び出し(関数呼び出し)を多用するエージェント用途では、ToolMessageやtool_callsの整合性が崩れると、途中状態の復元やデバッグ、ログの再現が困難になりやすい。今回の修正は、こうした場面での信頼性向上に寄与すると見られる。

langchain-perplexityは、LangChainが採用するパートナーパッケージ方式の一つで、各種モデルプロバイダーとの連携を本体から切り離して個別に提供する仕組みに沿っている。OpenAIやAnthropic、Googleなど他社向けにも同様の連携パッケージが用意されており、提供元ごとに独立したリリースサイクルで更新が進められている。Perplexityは検索を組み合わせた応答に強みを持つとされ、こうした連携を通じてLangChainベースのアプリケーションから利用しやすくなっている。

バージョン1.3.1からの変更はこの修正のみで、新機能の追加や互換性に影響する大きな変更は含まれていないとされる。ツール呼び出しを伴うワークフローでシリアライズ関連の問題に遭遇していた利用者にとっては、早めの更新を検討する価値があるだろう。
789ae57829cd1b90.bodyEn:
The LangChain ecosystem has published langchain-perplexity 1.3.2, a small patch release whose single notable change is a fix for incorrect serialization of ToolMessage and AIMessage.tool_calls. While narrow in scope, the update matters to anyone building agentic applications on top of Perplexity's models, because reliable serialization of tool-calling messages is foundational to persisting, replaying, and transmitting agent state.

langchain-perplexity is one of the many provider integration packages that LangChain maintains alongside its core libraries. Rather than bundling every model provider into a single monolithic dependency, LangChain splits integrations into separate packages such as langchain-openai, langchain-anthropic, and langchain-perplexity. This modular approach lets each integration version independently and ship fixes without forcing a full framework upgrade. The package wraps Perplexity's API, which is notable for combining large language models with live web search, exposing it through LangChain's standard chat model interface so it can be swapped in alongside other providers.

The bug addressed here concerns serialization, the process of converting in-memory objects into a format that can be stored or transmitted, typically JSON, and later reconstructed. In LangChain, messages are represented by typed objects. An AIMessage represents a model's response and can carry a tool_calls attribute, a structured list describing which tools or functions the model wants to invoke and with what arguments. A ToolMessage represents the result returned after a tool runs, and it is fed back into the conversation so the model can continue reasoning. These two message types are the backbone of tool calling, the mechanism that lets a model request external actions such as a database query, an API call, or a calculation, rather than only producing free-form text.

When serialization of these objects does not work correctly, the consequences tend to surface in places where messages cross a boundary. Examples include writing conversation history to a checkpoint store, sending state between processes or over a network, caching intermediate results, or logging traces for debugging. If a ToolMessage or the tool_calls payload on an AIMessage is not serialized faithfully, an application may lose the structured details of a tool invocation, fail to round-trip a conversation, or raise errors when attempting to reload prior state. For agent frameworks that depend on durable, replayable execution, such defects can be disruptive even when they appear minor. The release notes indicate this fix is the only change since version 1.3.1, which suggests the maintainers intended a targeted correction rather than a broader update.

This kind of patch reflects a wider pattern in the LangChain project, which has moved toward standardized message schemas and serialization conventions across its integrations. LangChain provides a serialization framework built around what it calls Serializable objects and a load and dump mechanism, intended to give a consistent representation regardless of which provider produced a message. Because provider packages must each conform to that shared contract, small discrepancies in how a given integration emits tool-call data can lead to exactly the sort of mismatch this release corrects. Keeping these representations consistent is increasingly important as more developers persist agent state in databases or use tools like LangGraph, LangChain's library for building stateful, graph-structured agent workflows that rely heavily on checkpointing and resumable execution.

The broader context is an industry-wide push toward tool-calling agents, where models are given access to external capabilities and orchestrated through multi-step loops. Standardized function and tool calling has become a common feature across major model providers, and emerging efforts such as the Model Context Protocol aim to formalize how tools and context are exchanged. In that environment, the fidelity of message serialization is not a peripheral concern but a prerequisite for interoperability, observability through tools like LangSmith, and reproducible behavior.

For practitioners, the practical guidance appears straightforward. Teams using langchain-perplexity with tool-calling workflows, particularly those that serialize or persist conversation history, are likely to benefit from upgrading to 1.3.2. Because the release contains only this fix and no documented behavioral changes to model invocation, the upgrade risk should be low, though users are generally advised to validate against their own test suites. As always with patch releases, reviewing the official changelog before deploying remains good practice, especially in production agent systems where state durability is critical.

c893ddf8d7f5ce8e.bodyJa:
ZedエディタのGLSL拡張機能が、バージョンv0.2.4へとアップデートされた。シェーダ記述に用いるGLSL（OpenGL Shading Language）の編集支援を担う拡張で、今回は具体的なリリースノートを伴わない、ルーティンなメンテナンス更新と見られる。

GLSLは、GPU上で動作するシェーダプログラムを記述するためのC言語風の言語で、リアルタイムグラフィックスやゲーム開発、ビジュアルエフェクト、近年ではWebGLやシェーダアートの分野でも広く使われている。頂点シェーダやフラグメントシェーダといった処理を書く際に、構文ハイライトや補完が利けば、コードの可読性が高まり、記述ミスの早期発見にもつながりやすい。

Zedは、コードエディタAtomやTree-sitterの開発に関わったメンバーが立ち上げたZed Industriesによる、Rust製の高速エディタである。GPUレンダリングを前提とした描画性能や軽量な動作を特徴とし、機能の多くを拡張機能（extension）として後付けできる設計を採用している。GLSL拡張もその一つで、多くの言語拡張と同様に、構文解析の基盤としてTree-sitterを利用していると見られる。

今回のv0.2.4は、要約によれば特段の新機能や大きな仕様変更を含まない軽微な更新とされる。こうしたバージョンバンプは、依存ライブラリの更新や、エディタ本体のAPI変更への追従、細かな不具合修正などを目的に行われることが多い。利用者側で操作感が大きく変わる可能性は低いとみられ、既存環境への影響は限定的だろう。

背景として、エディタの言語サポートは一度作って終わりではなく、対象言語の仕様変化やエディタ本体の進化に合わせて継続的に手入れされていく性質がある。VS CodeをはじめとするほかのエディタでもGLSL向け拡張が提供されており、シェーダ開発環境の選択肢は着実に広がりつつある。地味ではあるが、こうした小刻みな更新の積み重ねこそが、拡張機能の安定性と長期的な信頼性を支えていると言える。
c893ddf8d7f5ce8e.bodyEn:
The GLSL extension for the Zed editor has been updated to version 0.2.4, a routine maintenance release that keeps language support for the OpenGL Shading Language in step with the editor's evolving extension platform. While incremental on its own, the update is a useful reminder of how modern editors increasingly rely on a constellation of small, independently versioned plug-ins to deliver language-specific tooling.

GLSL, the OpenGL Shading Language, is a C-like language used to write shaders, the small programs that run on a GPU to control how vertices and pixels are processed during rendering. It is central to real-time graphics work in OpenGL and WebGL, and, by way of cross-compilation, parts of the Vulkan ecosystem. Developers working on games, visual effects, scientific visualization, and creative coding tools frequently edit .glsl, .vert, .frag, and related files, and a dedicated editor extension provides the syntax highlighting, bracket matching, and structural awareness that make those files easier to read and navigate.

In Zed, extensions like this one typically supply a Tree-sitter grammar and the configuration that maps it to file types, along with query files that drive syntax highlighting and code folding. Zed, a Rust-based editor developed by Zed Industries, builds its extension system around Tree-sitter parsers and WebAssembly modules, allowing third-party language support to be distributed through the editor's extension registry rather than baked into the core application. This separation lets a grammar or language extension iterate on its own schedule, which is precisely what a version bump like v0.2.4 represents.

Because the release ships without detailed notes, the specific contents of the update are not publicly enumerated. Changes of this kind are commonly limited to refreshing a pinned Tree-sitter grammar revision, adjusting the extension manifest for compatibility with a newer Zed extension API, correcting file-type associations, or tidying highlight queries. The increment to 0.2.4 follows semantic versioning conventions, where the trailing number generally signals backward-compatible fixes or minor adjustments rather than new user-facing features. In the absence of a changelog, it is reasonable to treat this as housekeeping that keeps the extension installable and functional against current builds of the editor.

For users, the practical impact is likely to be minimal and mostly invisible. The extension should continue to recognize shader files and apply highlighting as before, with any underlying fixes applied the next time the extension updates. Those who manage Zed through its built-in extensions panel will generally receive the new version without manual intervention, while anyone maintaining a forked or locally installed copy may need to pull the latest revision to stay aligned.

The update also fits a broader pattern across the editor landscape. Tree-sitter, originally developed at GitHub, has become a de facto standard for incremental parsing and is used by Neovim, Helix, Emacs, and other tools, which means GLSL grammars and related queries are often shared or adapted across ecosystems. Comprehensive shader tooling frequently goes a step further by pairing such grammars with a language server; in the GLSL space, projects like glsl_analyzer provide diagnostics, completion, and hover information through the Language Server Protocol. A syntax-focused extension such as this one is typically a prerequisite layer that a language server can complement, rather than a replacement for it.

Zed itself has been moving steadily toward a more open, community-driven model, having released its core under permissive licensing and opened its extension registry to outside contributors. Frequent, low-ceremony version bumps to language extensions are a natural consequence of that approach, and they tend to accelerate as the editor's extension API matures and occasionally introduces changes that downstream packages must track. Seen in that light, glsl v0.2.4 is unremarkable in scope but representative of the ongoing maintenance that keeps a growing catalog of language extensions healthy.

For graphics developers evaluating Zed as a shader-editing environment, the takeaway is continuity: GLSL support remains actively maintained, and routine releases like this one suggest the extension is being kept current rather than left to drift. Users seeking richer features beyond highlighting should consider pairing it with an appropriate language server and confirm file-type coverage for their particular project layout before committing to a workflow.

0848da59f45ef713.bodyJa:
ローカルでLLMを動かすためのツール「Ollama」の最新リリース候補版「v0.30.6-rc0」が公開された。今回の事前リリースにおける主要な変更点は、Raspberry Pi向けの起動サポート「oh-my-pi」（#16410）の追加である。

Ollamaは、大規模言語モデル（LLM）をクラウドではなく手元のPCやサーバー上で実行できるようにするオープンソースのツールだ。内部的にはllama.cppなどの推論エンジンを活用し、GGUF形式のモデルを簡単なコマンドで取得・実行できる手軽さから、プライバシーを重視する用途やオフライン環境での利用を中心に支持を広げてきた。

今回の「rc0」はリリース候補版（release candidate）であり、正式版の前段階として不具合の洗い出しや動作検証を目的に配布されるものだ。そのため本番環境への導入には慎重さが求められる一方、新機能をいち早く試したい開発者にとっては検証の機会となる。

注目される「oh-my-pi」は、その名称からRaspberry Pi上でのOllama起動を支援する仕組みと見られる。Raspberry PiはARMベースの安価なシングルボードコンピューターで、教育やIoT、組み込み用途で広く使われている。限られたメモリやCPU資源の中でLLMを動かすには制約が大きいものの、エッジ環境でのローカル推論ニーズの高まりを背景に、小型デバイスへの対応を強化する動きと位置づけられる可能性がある。

ローカルLLMの分野では、LM StudioやGPT4Allといった選択肢に加え、Ollama自身もモデルのダウンロードからAPI提供までを一括で担う点で存在感を高めている。今回のRaspberry Pi対応がどの程度の実用性を備えるかは、正式版での仕様確定や実機での検証を待つ必要がある。利用を検討する場合は、リリースノートや関連するプルリクエスト（#16410）の内容を確認したうえで判断するのが望ましい。
0848da59f45ef713.bodyEn:
Ollama has published v0.30.6-rc0, a release candidate for the next iteration of its widely used local large language model runtime. The headline change in this pre-release is the addition of launch support for Raspberry Pi hardware, tracked internally as the "oh-my-pi" feature (pull request #16410). For developers and hobbyists interested in running language models on inexpensive single-board computers, the update signals continued attention to the lower end of the hardware spectrum rather than only high-powered GPUs.

Ollama is an open-source tool that simplifies downloading, managing, and running open-weight language models on a local machine. It provides a command-line interface, a REST API, and a model library that packages weights along with configuration in a single pull command. Under the hood it builds on the llama.cpp inference engine, which is known for efficient CPU and GPU execution across a range of platforms. Because Ollama abstracts away much of the setup complexity, it has become a common entry point for people who want to experiment with models such as Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen without relying on cloud APIs.

A release candidate, denoted here by the "rc0" suffix, is a build that the maintainers consider close to final but want to expose to broader testing before a stable tag. Users who install a release candidate are effectively helping validate the changes against real workloads and diverse hardware. It is generally advisable to treat such builds as provisional, since regressions or last-minute fixes can occur before the corresponding stable version, in this case v0.30.6, is published. The fact that this candidate centers on a single primary change suggests a focused, incremental update rather than a sweeping overhaul.

The Raspberry Pi support is the most notable element of this candidate. The Raspberry Pi family consists of ARM-based single-board computers that are popular for education, embedded projects, and home servers, with recent models like the Raspberry Pi 5 offering meaningfully more compute and memory than earlier generations. Running language models on such constrained devices is challenging because memory capacity and bandwidth, rather than raw clock speed, often become the limiting factors. Launch support, as described here, appears to focus on getting Ollama to start and operate correctly in that environment, which is a prerequisite before users can reasonably evaluate inference performance. The exact scope of "oh-my-pi" beyond startup behavior is not fully detailed in the release note, so practical expectations should be tempered until the feature is exercised more widely.

This move fits a broader industry trend toward edge and on-device inference. Smaller, more efficient open models have proliferated, including quantized variants that compress weights to reduce memory footprint, making it feasible to run capable models on modest hardware. Quantization formats such as the GGUF files used by llama.cpp allow the same model to be offered at multiple precision levels, trading some accuracy for lower resource demands. On a Raspberry Pi, users would likely lean on heavily quantized, parameter-efficient models and accept slower token generation in exchange for fully local, private operation with no recurring cloud costs.

Ollama is not alone in this space. Alternatives and complementary projects include llama.cpp itself for those who prefer to work closer to the engine, LM Studio for a desktop graphical experience, and frameworks such as vLLM that target server-grade throughput. Hardware vendors have also pushed in the same direction, with ARM optimizing its libraries for AI workloads and NVIDIA promoting compact developer boards like the Jetson series for edge inference. Against that backdrop, extending Ollama's reach to the Raspberry Pi platform lowers the barrier further for tinkerers and educators who already own the hardware.

For those wishing to try the candidate, release candidates are typically available through Ollama's GitHub releases page and its standard installation channels, though users should confirm that their chosen method explicitly offers the rc0 build. Anyone running production or critical workflows is generally better served waiting for the stable v0.30.6 tag. Reviewing the full changelog and any accompanying notes is recommended, since additional fixes or smaller adjustments may accompany the highlighted Raspberry Pi work even when they are not called out in the summary. As always with pre-release software, backing up existing models and configurations before upgrading is a sensible precaution.

61f17448bf117e02.bodyJa:
AI コードエディタ「Cursor」が、ブラウザ上で UI を直接編集できる「デザインモード」を強化した。クリック、描画、音声による指示を通じて、AI エージェントがユーザーインターフェースを自動的に更新できるようになり、コードを直接書かずに視覚的な変更を反映させるフローが整いつつある。

今回の改善で中心となるのは、操作手段の多様化だ。これまでのテキストによる指示に加え、画面上の要素をクリックして対象を指定したり、変更したい範囲を描画して示したり、音声で意図を口頭で伝えたりできるようになったと説明されている。例えば「このボタンをもっと大きく」「この余白を詰めて」といった指示を、自然な形でエージェントに渡し、対応するコードの修正へとつなげることが想定される。

背景には、AI コーディング支援ツールが「コード生成」から「デザインと実装の橋渡し」へと領域を広げている流れがある。Cursor はもともと VS Code をベースにしたエディタとして AI 補完やエージェント機能を打ち出してきたが、ブラウザ機能を統合することで、実際に表示される画面を見ながら編集する体験を取り込もうとしていると見られる。視覚的な確認と修正を同じ環境内で完結できれば、デザイナーとエンジニアの間の往復コストを下げられる可能性がある。

こうした「見たまま」を起点にした UI 編集のアプローチは、競合領域でも注目されている。Vercel の v0 や各種スクリーンショットからコードを生成するツール、あるいは Figma のデザインデータを実装へ橋渡しする試みなど、デザインと実装の距離を縮める動きは各社で進んでいる。Cursor のデザインモードは、エディタ側にこの体験を取り込み、エージェントとの対話の中で完結させようとする点に特徴があるといえる。

音声入力に対応した点も、操作の幅を広げる要素として注目される。手を止めずに口頭で修正を指示できれば、試行錯誤を繰り返す UI 調整の場面でテンポを保ちやすくなると考えられる。一方で、クリックや描画による指示がどの程度正確にエージェントへ伝わり、意図通りの修正に結びつくかは、実際の使用感に左右される部分も大きい。今回の更新がデザイン作業の実務にどこまで定着するかは、今後の改良と利用者の評価を見ていく必要があるだろう。
61f17448bf117e02.bodyEn:
Cursor has expanded the capabilities of Design Mode in its built-in browser, allowing developers to direct AI agents to modify user interfaces through clicking, drawing, or speaking. The update matters because it tightens the loop between visual intent and code changes, addressing a long-standing friction point where front-end adjustments often require translating what a developer sees on screen into precise written instructions or manual edits.

Design Mode is a feature within the Cursor browser, the integrated web view that lets developers preview and interact with their running application without leaving the editor. According to the changelog, the enhanced mode now supports several input methods working together: users can click directly on an element they want to change, draw annotations to indicate regions or adjustments, or describe the desired outcome by voice. The agent then interprets these signals and updates the underlying UI code accordingly. The stated goal is a more intuitive editing flow, reducing the back-and-forth typically needed to communicate visual changes to an AI assistant.

The combination of pointing, sketching, and speaking reflects a broader move toward multimodal interaction in developer tools. Rather than relying solely on text prompts, the agent can ground its understanding in the actual rendered page. Clicking an element appears to give the agent a concrete reference point in the DOM, which can help it locate the correct component or style rule to modify. Drawing adds spatial context that is often difficult to express in words, such as indicating spacing, alignment, or which part of a layout should shift. Voice input lowers the barrier for describing changes quickly, though the practical accuracy of voice-driven edits is likely to depend on how clearly the intent maps to specific code.

For readers unfamiliar with the product, Cursor is an AI-centered code editor built on a fork of Visual Studio Code, developed by Anysphere. It integrates large language models to support code completion, chat-based assistance, and increasingly autonomous agents that can plan and apply multi-step changes across a codebase. The browser and Design Mode extend this agent model into the visual layer of web development, where the result of a change is something a developer needs to see rather than only read. This positions the feature within Cursor's wider effort to let agents operate on more of the development surface, from terminal commands to file edits and now interface adjustments.

The approach sits alongside a number of related industry efforts to bridge design and code. Tools such as Vercel's v0 generate UI components from text descriptions, Figma offers Dev Mode to hand off design specifications to engineers, and platforms like Webflow and Framer provide visual editing that produces production code. Browser-based inspection and live editing have also long existed in developer tools built into Chrome and Firefox, though those changes are typically not persisted back to source files. What distinguishes the agent-driven model is that the visual instruction is meant to flow back into the project's actual code, with the AI handling the translation. Whether this proves more reliable than manual editing will likely vary by project complexity and the structure of the codebase.

Several practical considerations remain relevant. Agent-applied UI changes generally benefit from review, since interpreting a drawn annotation or a spoken phrase introduces ambiguity that a model must resolve. Developers working with component libraries, design systems, or CSS frameworks may find that the quality of results depends on how consistently their code is organized, as the agent needs to identify the right place to make an edit. The changelog frames the update as an improvement to an existing capability rather than a wholly new system, suggesting incremental refinement of how the browser, Design Mode, and the agent coordinate.

For teams already using Cursor, the enhanced Design Mode offers a lower-friction path for iterating on interfaces, particularly for small visual tweaks that are tedious to specify in text. As with other agentic features, its value will become clearer through everyday use, and developers are likely to combine it with conventional editing rather than replace established workflows outright. The feature reflects a continuing trend of AI assistants moving closer to the surfaces where developers actually work, capturing intent through the same visual cues a person would naturally use.

c2f697d37bc610c0.bodyJa:
All Hands AI が開発する自律型ソフトウェア開発エージェント「OpenHands」のクラウド版に、パッチリリースとなる cloud 1.37.3 が公開された。今回の更新は機能追加ではなく、データベース周りの内部改善を中心とした保守的なリリースである。

主な変更点は、課題管理上「PLTF-2895」として追跡されていた event_callback テーブルのインデックス生成方式の見直しだ（プルリクエスト #14651）。具体的には、インデックスの作成を通常の CREATE INDEX を用いる形へ切り替えている。OpenHands はバックエンドに PostgreSQL を採用しているとみられ、エージェントの実行履歴やコールバックイベントといったデータの管理にこうしたテーブルが用いられる。

PostgreSQL では、インデックスを作成する手段として通常の CREATE INDEX のほかに、書き込みをブロックせずに作成できる CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY が存在する。後者はテーブルへの書き込みを止めずに済む利点がある一方で、トランザクションブロックの内側で実行できないという制約があり、Alembic などのマイグレーションツールと組み合わせた際にエラーや適用失敗を招くことがある。今回の変更は、こうしたマイグレーション実行時の安定性を高めることを意図したものと考えられる。

一般に、通常の CREATE INDEX はインデックス作成中に対象テーブルへの書き込みロックを伴うため、大規模なテーブルでは一時的な影響が生じうる。一方で、処理がトランザクション内で完結し、マイグレーションの整合性を担保しやすいという利点もある。どちらの方式が適切かは、対象テーブルの規模や運用状況によって変わってくる。

OpenHands は旧称 OpenDevin として知られ、Devin（Cognition）や GitHub Copilot のエージェント機能などと並び、コード生成にとどまらずタスクを自律的に遂行する「AI エージェント」分野で注目を集めるプロジェクトだ。今回のようなパッチリリースは派手さこそないものの、クラウドサービスの信頼性やデータベース運用の安全性を地道に底上げするものといえる。利用者は通常、特別な操作なく改善の恩恵を受けられると見られる。
c2f697d37bc610c0.bodyEn:
OpenHands has published cloud-1.37.3, a patch release for its hosted AI software development platform that centers on a single database-focused change. While modest in scope, the update is the kind of operational refinement that helps keep a high-traffic, agent-driven service stable, and it offers a useful window into how the team manages schema changes in production.

The headline item, tracked internally as PLTF-2895 and merged in pull request #14651, changes the way an index is created on the event_callback table so that it uses a plain CREATE INDEX statement. The release note is terse, but the phrasing strongly implies a move away from PostgreSQL's CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY variant toward the standard, blocking form of the command.

The distinction matters in practice. In PostgreSQL, a plain CREATE INDEX takes a lock that blocks writes to the affected table for the duration of the build, whereas CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY allows reads and writes to continue while the index is constructed. The concurrent option sounds strictly preferable, but it carries trade-offs: it generally takes longer, scans the table more than once, cannot run inside a transaction block, and can leave behind an invalid index if the operation fails partway through. Because it cannot be wrapped in a transaction, it also interacts awkwardly with migration frameworks that run each schema change inside one.

Given those constraints, the decision to use a plain CREATE INDEX appears to prioritize predictability and clean migration behavior over fully online, zero-lock index building. This is a common pattern in operational engineering: teams often reach for CONCURRENTLY first to avoid locking, then revert to the simpler statement when the table is small enough that any write lock is brief, or when a failed concurrent build has caused migration or cleanup problems. The exact motivation is not spelled out in the release, so the reasoning here is inferred from the change itself rather than stated by the maintainers.

The event_callback table is not described in the notes, but its name suggests it stores records tied to event callbacks, the mechanism by which the platform signals external systems or internal services when something happens during an agent run. Index changes on such a table can affect query performance for lookups and the cost of inserts, which is why even a small adjustment to how the index is built can be worth a dedicated patch.

For context, OpenHands, formerly known as OpenDevin, is an open-source platform for AI agents that write and execute code, run shell commands, and interact with browsers and APIs to complete software engineering tasks. OpenHands Cloud is the managed, hosted offering built on the same core. Because the cloud service runs continuously and serves many concurrent sessions, the team has to be deliberate about how database migrations are applied, since a long table lock during a deploy could stall active agent workloads.

As a patch release, the third in the 1.37 line, cloud-1.37.3 follows semantic versioning conventions that signal a backward-compatible fix rather than new features or breaking changes. Releases of this type are typically deployed with minimal disruption and are often invisible to end users, who would notice them mainly through improved reliability rather than any change in behavior.

The update also sits within a broader, well-established discipline around online schema changes. Python-based projects like OpenHands commonly manage database structure with migration tools such as Alembic, while the wider ecosystem includes Flyway and Liquibase for versioned migrations, and utilities like pg_repack for rebuilding tables and indexes with reduced locking. In the MySQL world, comparable concerns are addressed by tools such as gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change. The recurring theme across all of them is the tension between minimizing lock time and keeping migrations simple, transactional, and easy to roll back.

For operators and contributors tracking the project, the practical takeaway is straightforward: cloud-1.37.3 is a targeted database maintenance release with no indication of user-facing functional changes. Anyone running self-hosted deployments or following the release stream may want to review the linked pull request for the specific migration details, particularly if they have customized their schema or maintain their own index strategy on the event_callback table. As always with patch releases, the value lies less in headline capability and more in the steady operational hardening that keeps an active platform dependable.

2aeba9c6c9751879.bodyJa:
クラウドだけに依存しないAI開発が広がるなか、Microsoftはデバイス上やエッジ環境でモデルを動かす「Foundry Local」を打ち出している。応答速度やプライバシー、オフライン動作といった課題に、ローカル推論で応えようとする取り組みだ。

AIはもはやクラウド上の実験にとどまらない。開発者はアプリやデバイス、エッジシステムの内部にAIを組み込むことを求められつつあり、そこでは低遅延の応答性、データを外部に送らないプライバシー保護、ネットワークがなくても動くオフライン対応が重要になる。クラウドのAPIを呼ぶ方式では、通信のたびに遅延やコストが生じ、機微なデータが外部に出る懸念も残る。

Foundry Localは、こうした課題に対してモデルをローカル環境で実行する仕組みを提供する。MicrosoftのAI開発基盤であるFoundryの一部として位置づけられ、推論にはONNX Runtimeを活用すると見られる。CPUだけでなくGPUやNPUといった多様なハードウェアに対応し、デバイスの性能に応じて実行先を選べる設計が想定される。これにより、小型の言語モデル(SLM)を端末上で動かし、クラウドとの役割分担を柔軟に組める。

背景には、近年のオンデバイスAIの急速な広がりがある。MicrosoftはPhiシリーズのような軽量モデルを公開しており、限られた計算資源でも実用的な推論を目指してきた。同様の流れは業界全体に及び、ローカルでLLMを手軽に動かすOllamaやLM Studio、スマートフォン向けに最適化されたGoogleのGemini NanoやAppleのオンデバイス機能など、選択肢は増えている。半導体側でもNPUを搭載したPCが普及し、エッジ推論の土台が整いつつある。

開発者にとっての利点は、クラウドと近い開発体験を保ちながら、配置先を柔軟に選べる点にあるとされる。プロトタイプはローカルで素早く検証し、本番ではエッジとクラウドを使い分けるといった運用が考えられる。一方で、ローカル実行はデバイスの計算能力やメモリに制約され、大規模モデルをそのまま動かすのは難しい場合もある。用途に応じてモデルの規模や量子化を見極める設計判断が、引き続き重要になりそうだ。
2aeba9c6c9751879.bodyEn:
Edge AI development has long sat at an awkward intersection of ambition and constraint. AI is no longer confined to cloud experiments, and developers are increasingly expected to deliver intelligent features inside apps, devices, and edge systems where responsiveness, privacy, and offline reliability cannot be compromised. Microsoft Foundry Local is positioned to address that gap, offering a way to run models directly on local hardware rather than routing every inference request to a remote endpoint.

The core argument behind on-device AI is straightforward. Sending data to the cloud introduces latency, depends on a stable network connection, and can raise privacy or compliance concerns when sensitive information leaves the device. For interactive scenarios such as real-time assistants, document analysis, or industrial monitoring, even modest round-trip delays degrade the user experience. Running inference locally keeps data on the machine, removes the network as a single point of failure, and can reduce ongoing cloud inference costs. These benefits matter most in regulated industries, in environments with intermittent connectivity, and in consumer applications where users expect instant responses.

Foundry Local is Microsoft's answer to these requirements within the broader Foundry ecosystem, formerly known as Azure AI Foundry. It provides a local runtime for executing language and other models on a developer's own hardware, exposing them through interfaces that are intended to feel familiar to anyone who has worked with cloud-based model APIs. In practice this typically means a command-line interface for managing and running models, along with an SDK and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint so existing application code can be pointed at a local server with minimal changes. That compatibility is significant, because it lowers the cost of moving a prototype built against a cloud API toward an on-device deployment.

Under the hood, local inference performance depends heavily on hardware acceleration, and Foundry Local appears to lean on Microsoft's established inference stack to take advantage of available silicon. ONNX Runtime has been the company's primary engine for optimized model execution across CPUs, GPUs, and increasingly neural processing units, or NPUs. The arrival of NPUs in mainstream laptops, including the Copilot+ PC category, has made on-device inference far more practical than it was a few years ago, allowing models to run efficiently without draining battery or saturating the main processor. Foundry Local is likely designed to detect and use the most suitable accelerator on a given machine, selecting an appropriate model variant for the hardware it finds.

The tool fits alongside several adjacent efforts that together describe Microsoft's edge AI strategy. Windows AI Foundry and the Windows Copilot Runtime aim to expose AI capabilities to applications running on Windows, while smaller, efficient model families such as the Phi series are explicitly built to perform well within the memory and compute limits of local devices. The wider industry is moving in the same direction. Quantization techniques, which shrink models by reducing numerical precision, and formats such as GGUF popularized by community runtimes like llama.cpp and Ollama have made it realistic to run capable models on consumer hardware. Foundry Local enters a space where developers already have options, and its distinguishing value is likely its integration with the rest of the Microsoft and Azure tooling that many enterprises already use.

For teams evaluating the approach, a few practical considerations remain. Local models are generally smaller than their largest cloud counterparts, so there is a trade-off between capability and the resources a device can provide. Managing model versions, updates, and consistency across a fleet of varied hardware introduces operational complexity that cloud deployment avoids. A common pattern that appears to be emerging is hybrid: handling routine or privacy-sensitive work on the device while escalating more demanding requests to the cloud, which lets applications balance cost, speed, and quality.

The broader context is a steady shift from treating AI as a centralized service toward treating it as a capability that runs wherever computation happens to be. Foundry Local reflects that shift and gives developers a Microsoft-supported path to experiment with on-device inference using tools and interfaces consistent with cloud workflows. Whether it becomes a default choice will depend on how its performance, model selection, and lifecycle management compare with the growing field of local inference options, but it signals clear investment in edge AI as a first-class scenario rather than an afterthought.

0402204e9999054f.bodyJa:
ローカルLLM実行環境として広く使われるOllamaが、開発版となる「v0.30.5-rc0」を公開した。内部で推論エンジンとして利用するllama.cppをビルド「b9509」へ更新し、Gemmaのマルチモーダルモデルで報告されていたクラッシュを修正した点が主眼となる。

今回の修正の中心は、Gemma 4 12Bのマルチモーダルプロジェクターで発生していたゼロ除算クラッシュだ。画像などの入力をテキストモデルが扱える表現へ変換するプロジェクター部分で、ヘッド数を示すパラメータ「n_head」が0として扱われ、内部計算で0による除算が起きてプロセスが異常終了していたと見られる。この不具合はx86環境かつCUDAを用いるLinuxおよびWindowsのユーザーで顕在化していたとされ、該当する構成でGemmaのマルチモーダル機能を使う場合に影響が出ていた。

Ollamaはモデルのダウンロードから実行までを簡便に扱えるツールで、実際の推論処理の多くをllama.cppに委ねている。llama.cppはC/C++で実装されたオープンソースの推論ライブラリで、量子化やGPUオフロードなど幅広い最適化を備え、活発に更新が続いている。Ollamaが定期的にllama.cppのバージョンを引き上げているのは、こうした上流の改善やバグ修正を取り込むためであり、今回のクラッシュ修正もその一例といえる。

対象となったGemmaは、Googleが公開する軽量なオープンモデル群で、テキストに加えて画像を扱えるマルチモーダル対応版も提供されている。マルチモーダルでは、視覚エンコーダの出力を言語モデル側へ橋渡しするプロジェクターが重要な役割を担うが、モデルの構成情報の読み取りや初期化に不整合があると、今回のようなゼロ除算といった境界条件のバグにつながりやすい。

なお「rc0」という名称が示すとおり、本バージョンはリリース候補(release candidate)であり、正式版前の検証を目的とした位置づけと考えられる。安定性を重視する利用者は正式リリースを待つ選択肢もあるが、Gemmaのマルチモーダル利用で同様のクラッシュに直面していた場合は、この開発版で回避できる可能性がある。導入の際は、自身の環境がx86やCUDAなど該当条件に当てはまるかを確認したうえで判断するとよいだろう。
0402204e9999054f.bodyEn:
Ollama has issued v0.30.5-rc0, a release candidate whose primary purpose is to update the bundled llama.cpp inference engine and resolve a crash that affected users running Google's Gemma vision models on local hardware. The fix matters because the defect caused a hard failure — a divide-by-zero fault — that terminated the process rather than returning an error or falling back, interrupting any pipeline relying on combined image and text input.

The release advances llama.cpp to build b9509. Ollama is a packaging and serving layer that wraps llama.cpp, the C/C++ project that carries out the actual tensor computation and model loading. Because Ollama depends so directly on this engine, its capabilities and bug surface move in step with the upstream build it ships; bumping to b9509 brings in the relevant patch along with other upstream changes accumulated since the previous pinned version. The work is tracked under pull request #16511.

According to the release notes, the crash originated in the multimodal projector for Gemma 4 12B. In a vision-language model, the projector is the bridge that converts features from an image encoder into vectors the language model can consume alongside text tokens. The reported trigger was a configuration value of n_head=0, a head count of zero for the attention computation. Code that derives a per-head dimension by dividing the embedding width by the number of heads will fault when that denominator is zero, which is the divide-by-zero condition the patch addresses.

The summary scopes the impact to x86 systems using CUDA acceleration on Linux and Windows, meaning users with NVIDIA GPUs were the most likely to encounter it. That detail suggests the problem surfaced along a particular code path rather than across every backend, though the underlying configuration issue could in principle affect other setups; the published notes emphasize the x86/CUDA combination.

Some background helps frame why this is more than a routine patch. Gemma is Google's family of open-weight models, and its multimodal members accept images in addition to text, which expands their use beyond plain chat into tasks such as describing or reasoning over pictures. Running such models locally is exactly the scenario Ollama targets, and the projector is a prerequisite piece: without it, the visual half of the model cannot communicate with the language half. A crash in that component effectively blocks the multimodal feature for the affected model size.

It is worth noting the "rc0" suffix. This is a release candidate, an intermediate build offered ahead of a stable tag so that users can verify fixes before they are finalized. Teams that hit the Gemma crash may want to test this candidate, while others may prefer to wait for the corresponding stable release. Release candidates are common in fast-moving local-model tooling, where upstream engines like llama.cpp publish frequent builds and downstream projects must decide when to adopt them.
